children.title: Wireshark Hex Dump — Ethernet/IP/TCP Header Fields
children.label: Wireshark Hex Dump
children.summary: Reading a raw packet hex dump means knowing exactly how many bytes each header field consumes and in what order they appear.
children.core_idea:
Reading a raw packet hex dump means knowing exactly how many bytes each header field consumes and in what order they appear. This is the same content Wireshark parses automatically — but understanding it by hand is essential for interpreting raw captures, writing packet parsers, and CTF-style forensics challenges.

### Ethernet Header (14 bytes)
| Bytes | Field | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Destination MAC | `54:83:3a:b4:72:4a` |
| 6 | Source MAC | `38:87:d5:52:29:f2` |
| 2 | EtherType | `0800` = IPv4 |

### IPv4 Header (20+ bytes)
| Bytes | Field | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Version/IHL | `48` | Version=4, IHL=8 (32-bit words → 32 byte header w/ options) |
| 1 | (part of ToS) | | |
| 2 | Total Length | `0040` = 64 | IP header + TCP header (+ data) |
| 2 | Identification | `546c` | Used to reassemble fragments |
| 2 | Flags/Fragment Offset | `4000` | Flags=010 → Don't Fragment |
| 1 | TTL | `19` = 25 | Hop limit |
| 1 | Protocol | `06` | 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP, 1 = ICMP |
| 2 | Header Checksum | `01af` | |
| 4 | Source IP | `c0a8 0173` = 192.168.1.115 | |
| 4 | Destination IP | `22d9 ed5b` = 34.217.237.91 | |
| var | Options | present when IHL > 5 | |

### TCP Header (20+ bytes)
| Bytes | Field | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Source Port | `f581` = 62849 | |
| 2 | Destination Port | `0050` = 80 (HTTP) | |
| 4 | Sequence Number | `57c9 40bc` | |
| 4 | Acknowledgment Number | `ab98 037c` | |
| 1 | Data Offset/Flags (high nibble) | `80` | Data Offset=8 → 32-byte TCP header (has options) |
| 1 | Flags (low bits) | `14` | ACK + RST set |
| 2 | Window Size | `0400` | Flow-control receive window |
| 2 | Checksum | `d276` | |
| 2 | Urgent Pointer | `0000` | |
| var | Options | `0204 05b4 0103 0308 0101 0402` | MSS, window scale, SACK permitted, NOP, timestamps |

**Reading tip:** work outward-in — Ethernet header is always the first 14 bytes, then use the IHL nibble to find where the IP header ends, then use the TCP Data Offset nibble to find where the TCP header ends and payload begins.

children.title: DNS Resolution, Record Types & Zone Transfers
children.label: DNS Resolution, Record Types
children.summary: How DNS name resolution works, the record types involved, and why exposed zone transfers are a reconnaissance goldmine.
children.core_idea:
### How Resolution Works
1. Client queries a **recursive resolver** (often the ISP's or a public one like `1.1.1.1`)
2. Resolver walks the hierarchy: root servers → TLD servers (`.com`, `.edu`) → authoritative name servers for the domain
3. Authoritative server returns the record; resolver caches it per its **TTL** and returns the answer to the client

### Common Record Types
| Record | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **A** | Hostname → IPv4 address |
| **AAAA** | Hostname → IPv6 address |
| **CNAME** | Alias — points one hostname to another hostname (its *canonical name*), not directly to an IP |
| **MX** | Mail server(s) for the domain, with priority |
| **NS** | Authoritative name servers for the domain |
| **TXT** | Free-form text — commonly used for SPF/DKIM/DMARC policy strings and domain verification |
| **SOA** | Zone metadata — primary NS, refresh/retry/expire timers |

**Alias check:** if `nslookup`/`dig` on a hostname returns a **CNAME** pointing elsewhere before resolving to an IP, that hostname is an alias — its canonical name is whatever the CNAME points to.

### Zone Transfers (AXFR)
A **zone transfer** replicates an entire DNS zone from a primary to a secondary name server — legitimate for server-to-server sync, but if a server allows AXFR to *anyone*, an attacker can dump the full zone in one query, revealing every subdomain, internal hostnames, and network topology in one shot.

```
dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com
```

**Defense:** restrict transfers with an explicit `allow-transfer` ACL on the authoritative server (e.g. BIND) so only known secondary servers can pull the zone.

### Reconnaissance Angle
DNS is one of the richest free recon sources: subdomain enumeration (viewdns.info, `dnsdumpster`, certificate transparency logs via `crt.sh`), `whois` for registrant/admin contacts and netrange, and passive tools reveal third-party service dependencies (CDNs, email providers) that widen the attack surface without ever touching the target directly.

children.title: ICMP Diagnostics — ping & traceroute
children.label: ICMP Diagnostics
children.summary: ping tests host reachability and latency; traceroute maps the hop-by-hop path to a destination by sending packets with increasing TTL.
children.core_idea:
### ping — reachability & latency
Sends ICMP echo requests to test if two hosts can communicate and to measure round-trip time.

```
ping -c 3 www.iastate.edu
PING www.iastate.edu (20.241.39.52): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 20.241.39.52: icmp_seq=0 ttl=114 time=20.475 ms
```

- **Latency** — round-trip time per packet
- **Jitter** — variance in latency across packets; high jitter means an unstable path
- Packet loss and high loss rates degrade real-time media badly — streaming video becomes choppy around 2–10% loss and effectively unwatchable above ~50%, since players repeatedly stall to rebuffer

### traceroute — path discovery
Discovers the hop-by-hop route to a destination by sending packets with increasing **TTL** (time-to-live). Each router that decrements TTL to 0 drops the packet and returns a "Time Exceeded" ICMP message revealing its address — traceroute increments TTL by 1 each round to reveal the next hop.

```
traceroute 1.1.1.1
 1  _gateway (192.168.254.254)        0.55 ms
 2  routera-...iastate.edu             4.5 ms
 ...
14  one.one.one.one (1.1.1.1)          6.1 ms
```

- Asterisks (`*`) mean no response from that hop — the router may simply be configured not to reply to TTL-expired packets, not necessarily that it isn't forwarding traffic
- Some routers/firewalls block ICMP but still forward TCP — use **TCP-based traceroute** to get around this
- The same asymmetry (ICMP blocked, TCP allowed) is why ping sometimes fails through a firewall that a real TCP connection would pass through fine

### Related tools
- **iperf** — measures achievable bandwidth between two hosts
- **nmap** — port scanning to discover open services
- **tcpdump / Wireshark** — live packet capture for analyzing traffic, spotting attack traffic (e.g. a ping flood), and inspecting protocol fields directly

children.title: Routing Protocols — RIP, OSPF, BGP & Autonomous Systems
children.label: Routing Protocols
children.summary: An Autonomous System is a network under one administrative domain; interior protocols (RIP, OSPF) route within it, BGP routes between AS's.
children.core_idea:
### Autonomous Systems (AS)
A network (or group of networks) under a single administrative authority, identified by an AS number.
- **Stub AS** — connects to only one other AS (e.g. a single-homed business)
- **Multi-homed AS** — connects to multiple AS's but doesn't relay transit traffic between them
- **Transit AS** — connects multiple AS's and carries traffic on their behalf (ISP backbones)

### IGP vs EGP
- **IGP (Interior Gateway Protocol)** — routes within a single AS. Examples: RIP, OSPF
- **EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol)** — routes between AS's. Example: BGP

### RIP (Routing Information Protocol)
- **Distance-Vector** algorithm — each router shares its routing table with neighbors
- Runs over **UDP port 520**
- Metric = hop count, **max 15 hops**; **16 = infinity (unreachable)** — this caps RIP to small networks
- Vulnerable to routing loops; mitigated with **Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse**

### OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)
- **Link-State** algorithm — each router builds a full map of the network topology and runs Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm locally
- Runs directly over IP (protocol field = 89), not over TCP/UDP
- Converges faster and scales better than RIP; standard choice for interior routing in larger networks

### BGP (Border Gateway Protocol)
- **Path-Vector** algorithm — the protocol of the internet backbone, routes between AS's
- Runs over **TCP** (port 179) for reliable session establishment
- Policy-based, not purely shortest-path — routing decisions incorporate business relationships and administrative policy, not just path length

children.title: Distance-Vector Routing Loops & Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse
children.label: Distance
children.summary: Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse prevents a router from advertising a route back to the neighbor it learned that route from, stopping 2-node routing loops.
children.core_idea:
### The Problem
In distance-vector routing (e.g. RIP), if a link fails, neighboring routers can end up advertising stale routes to each other, creating a routing loop ("counting to infinity").

### Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse (SHPR)
**Rule:** For node **W**, its neighbor **X**, and destination **Y** — if W currently routes to Y *through* X (`H_WY = X`), then W reports `D_WY = ∞` in the distance-vector update it sends **specifically to X** (even though W's real internal distance to Y may not be infinity).

This prevents X from mistakenly using W as a path back toward Y after a failure, since W is telling X "I don't have a route to Y" (which is true from X's perspective — X shouldn't route through W to reach something W only knows about via X).

### Worked Example — Link 2–3 breaks
Topology: Node 1 ↔ Node 2 ↔ Node 3 ↔ Node 4, with Node 1 also reachable via Node 2.

| Iteration | Node 1's route to 4 | Node 2's route to 4 | Node 3's route to 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | via Node 2, dist 3 | via Node 3, dist 2 | via Node 4, dist 1 |
| After link 2–3 breaks | via Node 2, dist 3 | **unreachable (∞)** | via Node 4, dist 1 |
| Iteration 1 | **unreachable (∞)** | unreachable (∞) | via Node 4, dist 1 |
| Converged | unreachable (∞) | unreachable (∞) | via Node 4, dist 1 |

With SHPR, the loop resolves in one round because Node 1 was already poisoning its route back to Node 2.

### Limitation
SHPR only eliminates loops between **exactly two nodes**. Loops spanning **three or more nodes** can still form and require the protocol to "count to infinity" (bounded by RIP's 16-hop limit) before converging.

children.title: TCP Segment Header & Control Bits
children.label: TCP Segment Header &
children.summary: The TCP header carries sequence/ack numbers, control flags, and the receive window that together implement reliable, ordered, flow-controlled delivery.
children.core_idea:
### Header Fields
| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Source / Destination Port | 16-bit port numbers identifying the endpoints |
| Sequence Number | Byte index of the first data byte in this segment |
| Acknowledgment Number | Byte index of the **next expected byte** — not the next expected segment |
| Data Offset | Header length in 32-bit words (accounts for options) |
| Control Bits | See below |
| Window | Receiver's advertised flow-control window (bytes it's willing to accept) |
| Checksum | Error detection over header + data |
| Urgent Pointer | Valid only if URG flag set |
| Options | MSS, window scaling, SACK-permitted, timestamps, NOP padding |

### Control Bits
| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **SYN** | Synchronize — initiates a connection, consumes 1 sequence number |
| **ACK** | Acknowledgment field is valid |
| **FIN** | Finish — gracefully closes a connection, consumes 1 sequence number |
| **RST** | Reset — abruptly terminates a connection (no handshake) |
| **PSH** | Push — deliver buffered data to the application immediately |
| **URG** | Urgent — Urgent Pointer field is valid |

### Acknowledgment Semantics
- TCP ACKs are **byte-indexed, not segment-indexed** — `ACK(20)` means "I've received everything through byte 19; I'm expecting byte 20 next"
- TCP ACKs are **cumulative** — one ACK confirms everything up to that point, even if several segments arrived since the last ACK
- A **duplicate ACK** (same ACK number repeated) is an implicit signal that a segment was lost or reordered — three duplicate ACKs conventionally triggers **Fast Retransmit** without waiting for a timeout

children.title: TCP Connection Lifecycle — Handshake, Teardown, SYN Flood
children.label: TCP Connection Lifecycle
children.summary: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK establishes a connection; a modified handshake (FIN/ACK exchanged independently per direction) tears it down.
children.core_idea:
### Establishing — Three-Way Handshake
```
       Client                                      Server
────────────────────────                      ──────────────────────
Send SYN, seq=x (ISN)  ──────────────────►
                                              Receive SYN, enter SYN queue
                        ◄──────────────────  Send SYN seq=y, ACK x+1
Receive SYN+ACK
Send ACK y+1            ──────────────────►
                                              Connection established
```
- **ISN** (Initial Sequence Number) — a byte index chosen independently by each side
- SYN and FIN each consume exactly 1 sequence number
- **TCB** (Transmission Control Block) — the server's per-connection state, allocated once a SYN arrives

### SYN Flood & SYN Cookies
When a server receives a SYN, it queues the half-open connection in its **SYN queue** while waiting for the final ACK. A **SYN flood** abuses this: the attacker sends a massive volume of SYNs and never completes the handshake, exhausting the queue and blocking legitimate connections — a classic DoS.

**Defense — SYN Cookies:** instead of allocating state on SYN, the server encodes the connection info into the SYN-ACK's sequence number itself:
```
y = [5-bit t][3-bit m][24-bit s]
  t = timestamp mod 32
  m = index into a small table of MSS values
  s = hash(server IP, server port, client IP, client port, t)
```
No memory is allocated until the client's final ACK arrives. On receipt, the server recomputes the hash to validate the cookie, checks `t` hasn't expired, and decodes `m` for the negotiated MSS — reconstructing connection state without ever having stored it.

### Terminating — Modified Handshake (Half-Duplex Close)
```
       Initiator                                  Peer
────────────────────────                      ──────────────────────
Send FIN seq=x          ──────────────────►
                                              Receive FIN, send ACK x+1
                        ◄──────────────────  [peer may still send data]
Receive ACK
                        ◄──────────────────  Send FIN seq=y, ACK x+1
Receive FIN+ACK
Send ACK y+1             ──────────────────►
                                              Connection fully closed
```
- Teardown is **half-duplex** — each direction closes independently. After sending FIN, a host can still *receive* data from the other side (a "half-close")
- The side that sends the final ACK enters **TIME_WAIT** before fully releasing the connection, to absorb any delayed duplicate segments

children.title: TCP RTO Estimation — Karn's & Jacobson's Algorithms
children.label: TCP RTO Estimation
children.summary: Accurately estimating the retransmission timeout requires solving ACK ambiguity (Karn's Algorithm) and accounting for RTT variance (Jacobson's Algorithm).
children.core_idea:
### Problem 1 — ACK Ambiguity
When a segment is retransmitted, an incoming ACK is ambiguous: is it acknowledging the original transmission or the retransmission? Assuming the wrong one skews the RTT estimate (too large or too small either way).

**Karn's Algorithm:**
1. Only update `RTT_EST` using samples from segments that were **not** retransmitted
2. Ignore RTT samples that involve any retransmitted segment
3. To avoid the RTO staying too small under sustained loss, **double the RTO on each retransmission**: `RTO = γ × RTO` (γ typically 2)
4. Keep doubling until a valid (non-retransmitted) sample arrives, then recompute RTO normally from the fresh `RTT_EST`

### Problem 2 — High Variance in RTT
A simple exponential moving average (`RTT_EST = α·RTT_EST + (1−α)·RTT_Sample`) captures the mean but ignores variance. Real RTT distributions have heavy tails, so a fixed multiple of the mean (e.g. `RTO = 2 × RTT_EST`) causes frequent spurious timeouts.

**Jacobson's Algorithm** tracks the mean **and** the deviation:
```
D_Sample = |RTT_EST − RTT_Sample|
RTT_EST  = 7/8 × RTT_EST + 1/8 × RTT_Sample     (α = 0.875)
D_EST    = 3/4 × D_EST   + 1/4 × D_Sample        (δ = 0.75)
RTO      = RTT_EST + 4 × D_EST                    (η = 4)
```
This replaces the naive `RTO = 2 × RTT_EST` with a variance-aware formula, dramatically reducing unnecessary retransmissions on high-jitter paths.

children.title: TCP Congestion Control — cwnd, Slow Start & Congestion Avoidance
children.label: TCP Congestion Control
children.summary: TCP probes for available bandwidth with an exponentially-growing congestion window (Slow Start), then switches to linear growth (Congestion Avoidance) once near capacity.
children.core_idea:
### Core Mechanism
TCP maintains a **congestion window (cwnd)** limiting how much unacknowledged data it can have in flight, separate from the receiver's flow-control window (**rwnd**). The actual send window is `swnd = min(rwnd, cwnd)`.

TCP has no direct visibility into network congestion, so it infers it indirectly: **packet loss is treated as a congestion signal**.

### Phase 1 — Slow Start (SS)
- `cwnd` starts at 1 MSS (default MSS often 536 bytes historically; commonly ~1460 bytes on modern Ethernet paths)
- Every RTT with no loss, `cwnd` **doubles** (exponential growth) — one MSS added per received ACK
- Continues until `cwnd` reaches **ssthresh** (slow-start threshold), at which point TCP switches to Congestion Avoidance

### Phase 2 — Congestion Avoidance (CA)
- Entered when `cwnd ≥ ssthresh`
- Each non-duplicate ACK: `cwnd ← cwnd + 1/⌊cwnd⌋` — net effect is **cwnd grows by ~1 MSS per RTT** (linear/additive growth)

```
cwnd
 ▲                          ssthresh
 │                    ┌───── (CA: +1/RTT, linear)
 │             ┌─────/
 │      ┌─────/
 │ ┌───/     (SS: doubles each RTT)
 │/
 └──────────────────────────────► time
```

A real capture typically shows this visually: a sharp exponential spike during Slow Start, followed by a "staircase" of small linear increments during Congestion Avoidance, with occasional sawtooth drops on loss events.

### Detecting Congestion
Congestion is inferred from either:
- **Timeout (RTO expiry)** — a strong congestion signal, treated aggressively
- **Triple duplicate ACK** — a weaker/faster signal that a single segment was lost, handled less aggressively (Fast Retransmit) since later segments are still arriving fine

children.title: TCP Congestion Control Variants — Tahoe, Reno, Vegas, CUBIC, BBR
children.label: TCP Congestion Control Variants
children.summary: Successive TCP variants respond to loss less destructively (Tahoe → Reno → CUBIC) or shift from loss-based to delay-based congestion signals (Vegas, BBR).
children.core_idea:
| Variant | Congestion Response | Key Idea |
|---|---|---|
| **Tahoe** | Any loss (timeout *or* dup ACK) → `cwnd = 1`, `ssthresh = cwnd/2`, restart Slow Start | Simple but destroys throughput on every single loss |
| **Reno** | Distinguishes RTO (full Tahoe-style reset) from triple-dup-ACK (**Fast Recovery**: halve cwnd and continue from there instead of dropping to 1) | Avoids over-reacting to isolated packet loss |
| **New Reno** | Improves Reno's Fast Recovery to correctly handle **partial ACKs** — multiple losses in one window no longer prematurely exit Fast Recovery | Better behavior under multiple losses per RTT |
| **Vegas** | Delay-based — compares actual throughput to expected throughput; increases/decreases cwnd based on how many packets appear to be queuing, *before* loss occurs | Proactive rather than reactive to congestion |
| **CUBIC** | Loss-based but backs off less aggressively (~20% cwnd cut vs. 50%) and grows cwnd along a cubic function of time since the last loss | Default on Linux; designed for high-bandwidth, high-latency ("long fat") networks |
| **BBR** | Model-based — estimates bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip propagation delay directly, then paces sending to match, rather than reacting to loss at all | Google's algorithm; avoids filling buffers (bufferbloat) that loss-based algorithms tolerate |

**Classification:** packet-loss-based algorithms (Tahoe/Reno/New Reno/CUBIC) treat loss as the congestion signal; delay-based algorithms (Vegas, BBR) watch for increasing latency as an earlier warning sign, aiming to avoid loss altogether rather than recover from it.

children.title: DHCP — Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
children.label: DHCP
children.summary: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses and configuration via a 4-step Discover/Offer/Request/ACK exchange, building on the older BOOTP protocol.
children.core_idea:
### Background — BOOTP
**BOOTP** (Bootstrap Protocol) let diskless workstations be remotely booted on a network by mapping a known MAC address to an IP assignment. Well-known UDP ports: **67** (server), **68** (client) — DHCP inherited these.

### DHCP
Builds on BOOTP to deliver full configuration information to a host and assign **temporary** IP addresses, letting ISPs and network admins maximize use of a limited address pool. **DHCPv6** uses UDP ports **547** (server) / **546** (client).

### 4-Step Operation (DORA)
1. **DHCP Discover** — host broadcasts, looking for any DHCP server
2. **DHCP Offer** — one or more servers reply with an offered IP + configuration
3. **DHCP Request** — host broadcasts, selecting one offer
4. **DHCP ACK** — the selected server confirms and allocates the IP for lease time **T**, along with subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers

### Lease Renewal Timers
- **T₁ = 0.5T** — host attempts to renew directly with the **original** server
- **T₂ = 0.875T** — if no renewal by T₂, host broadcasts to **any** server
- If no reply by **T**, the host must relinquish the address and restart DHCP from scratch

### Real-World Example (`ipconfig /all`)
```
Physical Address  : B0-7B-25-2C-6B-48   ← MAC (OUI = vendor prefix)
DHCP Enabled      : Yes
IPv4 Address      : 10.24.101.130
Subnet Mask       : 255.255.252.0
Default Gateway   : 10.24.103.254
DHCP Server       : 10.10.67.136
Lease Obtained / Expires : [timestamps]
DNS Servers       : [list]
```

### DHCP Starvation (attack)
An attacker rapidly requests every available address in the pool using spoofed MAC addresses, exhausting the DHCP server so legitimate clients can't get an IP — often paired with a rogue DHCP server to then hand out malicious gateway/DNS settings.

children.title: NAT — Network Address Translation
children.label: NAT
children.summary: NAT lets many private hosts share one public IP by rewriting the (IP, port) pair on outbound packets and maintaining a translation table to route replies back.
children.core_idea:
### Purpose
Converts between **private** and **global** IP addresses so multiple private hosts can share one public IP.

### Operation
- Internal hosts generate packets with **private IP + TCP/UDP port**
- The NAT router maps each **(private IP, port)** pair to a **(shared public IP, available port)** pair, recording the mapping in an **Address Translation Table**
- Return traffic is matched against the table and routed back to the correct internal host

```
Private Network              NAT Router                Public Network
192.168.0.10 : x   ──►   Address Translation   ──►   128.100.10.15 : y
192.168.0.13 : w   ──►         Table            ──►   128.100.10.15 : z
```

### Security Implication
NAT incidentally provides a thin layer of obscurity — internal hosts aren't directly addressable from the internet — but it is **not** a substitute for a firewall; it doesn't inspect or filter traffic content.

children.title: Ethernet — IEEE 802.3 MAC Frame Structure
children.label: Ethernet
children.summary: The Ethernet frame carries preamble, addressing, length, payload, padding and a CRC-based FCS, bounded to 64–1518 bytes.
children.core_idea:
### Frame Layout
```
| Preamble | SD | Dest Addr | Src Addr | Length | Information | Pad | FCS |
|    7     |  1 |     6     |    6     |   2    |   variable  | var |  4  |     (bytes)
                 <-------------- 64 – 1518 bytes -------------->
```

| Field | Size | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Preamble** | 7 bytes | Alternating `10101010` pattern for clock synchronization |
| **SD (Start Delimiter)** | 1 byte | Marks frame start (`10101011`) |
| **Destination / Source Address** | 6 bytes each | 48-bit MAC addresses |
| **Length** | 2 bytes | Size of the Information field (max 1500 bytes = `0x05DC`) |
| **Information** | variable | Payload |
| **Pad** | variable | Zero-padding to reach the 64-byte minimum frame size |
| **FCS** | 4 bytes | CRC-32 over addresses, length, information, and pad — the NIC discards frames that fail this check or have an invalid length |

### Physical Standards
| Standard | Medium | Max Segment | Topology |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10Base5 | Thick coax | 500 m | Bus |
| 10Base2 | Thin coax | 200 m | Bus |
| 10BaseT | Cat3 twisted pair | 100 m | Star |
| 100BaseT | Cat5 twisted pair | 100 m | Star |

### Hubs vs. Switches
| Device | Behavior | Collision Domain |
|---|---|---|
| **Hub** | Broadcasts every frame to all ports | Shared — one collision domain for the whole segment |
| **Switch** | Forwards frames only to the correct destination port (by MAC address) | Separate per port |

Hubs are physically wired as a star but behave like a shared bus; switches eliminate per-port collisions, which is why they replaced hubs almost entirely.

### Ethernet Timeline
1973 Metcalfe & Boggs invent Ethernet → 1985 IEEE 802.3 standard (10 Mbps) → 1995 Fast Ethernet (100 Mbps) → 1998 Gigabit → 2002 10 Gigabit → 2007 100 Gigabit. Ethernet remains the dominant LAN standard.

children.title: Medium Access Control — ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD
children.label: Medium Access Control
children.summary: Random-access MAC protocols coordinate loosely: ALOHA just sends and retries, CSMA senses the channel first, and CSMA/CD aborts early on collision to save bandwidth.
children.core_idea:
### Two Broad Approaches to Sharing a Medium
- **Static Channelization** — fixed, dedicated channels per user (used in satellite/cellular)
- **Dynamic Medium Access Control** — channels allocated on demand, either via **Scheduling** (coordinated, e.g. Token Ring) or **Random Access** (loose coordination — send, wait, retry)

### ALOHA
The simplest random-access scheme: transmit whenever you have data, retry on collision. The conceptual basis for CSMA and its descendants.

### CSMA (Carrier Sensing Multiple Access)
A station senses the channel before transmitting:
- **Idle** → transmit immediately
- **Busy** → wait, per variant:
  - **1-Persistent** — keep sensing, transmit the instant it goes idle (aggressive, high collision risk with multiple waiting stations)
  - **Non-Persistent** — wait a random backoff before sensing again (less aggressive, lower utilization, fewer collisions)

### CSMA/CD (Collision Detection)
Improves on CSMA by **aborting transmission immediately** on detecting a collision, instead of wasting bandwidth sending a doomed frame to completion:
1. Detect collision mid-transmission
2. Abort
3. Send a short **jamming signal** so all stations know a collision occurred
4. Apply a backoff algorithm before re-attempting

### Interconnection Devices by Layer
| Device | Layer | Function |
|---|---|---|
| Repeater | Physical (L1) | Amplifies/regenerates signal |
| Switch/Bridge | Data Link (L2) | Forwards frames by MAC address |
| Router | Network (L3) | Routes packets by IP address |
| Gateway | L4+ | Translates between different protocols/architectures |

children.title: OSI Model & Network Architectures
children.label: OSI Model & Network
children.summary: The OSI model's 7 layers separate concerns from physical bit transmission up through application services; real networks use circuit-, message-, or packet-switching.
children.core_idea:
### The 7 Layers (top to bottom)
| Layer | Transfers | Role |
|---|---|---|
| **Application** | — | Services required by end-user applications (closest to the user) |
| **Presentation** | — | Data formatting, encryption, compression |
| **Session** | — | Manages sessions/dialogs between hosts |
| **Transport** | Segments | End-to-end delivery — reliable stream (TCP: handshake, flow control, congestion control) or fast unreliable datagrams (UDP) |
| **Network** | Packets | Routing, addressing (IP) |
| **Data Link** | Frames | Error detection (CRC), flow control *(no congestion control — that's an end-to-end concept)*, Medium Access Control for shared LANs |
| **Physical** | Bits | Raw signal transmission |

### Network Architectures & Transfer Modes
- **Circuit switching** ("reserve and use") — automated switches establish a dedicated physical path for the whole call; classic telephone network
- **Message switching** ("store and forward") — telegraph-style; whole messages hop node to node
- **Packet switching** ("break and route") — modern internet; messages are broken into packets, each independently routed and reassembled at the destination

### Features of the Internet
A digital, global, packet-switched network of networks (WANs/LANs), organized as a layered architecture (OSI vs. the simpler TCP/IP 4-layer model in practice).

children.title: IP Subnetting — Masks, CIDR & Longest Prefix Match
children.label: IP Subnetting
children.summary: Subnetting borrows host-ID bits to create smaller networks; the subnet address is the bitwise AND of the IP and mask, and routers use longest-prefix match when multiple entries match.
children.core_idea:
### Core Formula
```
subnet address = IP address  AND  subnet mask
```

### Worked Example — Class B, need ≤100 hosts/subnet
Given network `150.100.0.0/16`, split into subnets of up to 100 hosts each:
- Need 7 host-ID bits → 2⁷ − 2 = **126 usable hosts** (comfortably covers 100)
- Remaining 16 − 7 = **9 bits** for subnet ID → up to 512 subnets, mask = `/25` = `255.255.255.128`

Find the subnet containing `150.100.12.176`:
```
IP:   10010110 01100100 00001100 10110000
Mask: 11111111 11111111 11111111 10000000   (/25)
AND:  10010110 01100100 00001100 10000000   = 150.100.12.128
```
- Directed broadcast: `150.100.12.255` (all host bits set to 1)
- Usable range: `150.100.12.129`–`150.100.12.254` (2⁷ − 2 = 126 hosts)

### Variable-Length Subnetting
Different departments can get different-sized subnets from the same block — e.g. from `195.100.20.0/24` (Class C): a 90-host department gets a `/25`, and two 60-host departments each get a `/26`. Subnets must never overlap; if remaining address space is oddly shaped, a department may need multiple smaller subnets rather than one contiguous block.

### Longest Prefix Match
When a packet's destination matches multiple routing table entries, the router picks the entry with the **most specific (longest) prefix**:
```
Dest         Mask   Next-hop
150.100.0.0   /16    R1
150.100.12.128 /25   R2

Packet to 150.100.12.176 matches both → routed via R2 (/25 wins over /16)
```

### Real-World Example (`10.24.101.130`, mask `/22`)
```
IP:   00001010 00011000 01100101 10000010
Mask: 11111111 11111111 11111100 00000000
AND:  00001010 00011000 01100100 00000000  = 10.24.100.0/22
```
Usable range: `10.24.100.1`–`10.24.103.254` (2¹⁰ − 2 = 1022 hosts).

children.title: Physical Layer — Line Coding Schemes
children.label: Physical Layer
children.summary: Line coding maps bits to physical signal levels; schemes trade off DC balance, clock recovery, and noise immunity differently.
children.core_idea:
Good line coding needs: **timing recovery**, low implementation complexity/cost, low power, noise immunity, and ideally built-in error detection.

| Scheme | Mapping | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|
| **Unipolar NRZ** | `1`→+A, `0`→0 | Simple but poor timing recovery, has a DC component |
| **Polar NRZ** | `1`→+A/2, `0`→−A/2 | Simple, energy efficient, better noise immunity — still poor timing recovery |
| **Bipolar** | `1` alternates +A/2/−A/2, `0`→0 | Zero DC component; long runs of zeros still lose sync (fixed with B8ZS/B6ZS/B3ZS substitution codes) |
| **Manchester (1B2B)** | `1`→+A/2→−A/2, `0`→−A/2→+A/2 (transition mid-bit) | Self-clocking, excellent timing recovery; coding rate is only 1/2 bit per pulse (10 Mbps needs 20 MHz baud) |
| **mBnL** | m bits → n pulses over L signal levels, constrained by 2^m ≤ Lⁿ | Coding rate = m/n; examples: 2B1Q (2²≤4¹), 4B3T (2⁴≤3³) |
| **NRZI** | `1`→transition at bit start, `0`→no transition | Differential (polarity-insensitive); errors tend to occur in pairs |
| **Differential Manchester** | `1`→no transition at start, `0`→transition at start, always a mid-bit transition | Polarity insensitive, excellent clock recovery, errors occur in pairs. Unlike plain Manchester, it's robust to accidental polarity inversion (+/− swapped) |

### Noise & Reliable Communication
- Noise limits amplitude-detection accuracy, restricts usable signal levels, and raises **Bit Error Rate (BER)**
- **SNR** = Average Signal Power / Average Noise Power; larger SNR → lower BER. In decibels: `SNR(dB) = 10·log₁₀(SNR)`

### Shannon Channel Capacity
```
C = W · log₂(1 + SNR)   bps
```
where `W` = bandwidth (Hz). If the desired rate `R ≤ C`, arbitrarily reliable communication is achievable with sufficiently complex coding (BER can be made arbitrarily small); if `R > C`, reliable communication is **not possible** regardless of coding.

children.title: Error Detection & Recovery — CRC and ARQ
children.label: Error Detection & Recovery
children.summary: CRC appends check bits computed via polynomial division to detect transmission errors; ARQ protocols use ACK/NAK, retransmission, and sequence numbers to recover from them.
children.core_idea:
### CRC (Cyclic Redundancy Check)
Given `k` information bits, CRC generates `n − k` check bits by polynomial division, producing an `n`-bit codeword:
1. Represent the `k` info bits as an information polynomial `i(x)`
2. Multiply by `x^(n-k)` to make room for check bits, forming the dividend polynomial
3. Divide by a fixed generator polynomial `g(x)` (the divisor) using modulo-2 (XOR) arithmetic
4. The remainder becomes the check bits, appended to form the codeword polynomial
5. Transmit the resulting `n`-bit codeword
6. Receiver divides the received codeword by the same `g(x)` — a non-zero remainder means an error was detected

CRC can be implemented efficiently in hardware using a **shift register circuit** wired to perform the polynomial division on the fly.

### Error Vector & Undetectable Errors
`received = codeword XOR error_vector`. A CRC can only detect the error if the error polynomial isn't itself a multiple of the generator polynomial — this is why **certain even-numbered bit-error patterns**, and error bursts longer than the generator's degree, can occasionally slip through undetected. **FUE (Fraction of Undetectable Errors)** quantifies this residual risk for a given burst length `L`.

### ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)
Three design goals for a working ARQ protocol:
1. Deliver each frame **error-free**
2. Deliver each frame **exactly once** (no duplicates)
3. Deliver frames **in order**

Five basic elements: (1) error detection via CRC, (2) control frames — ACK required, NAK optional, (3) retransmission, (4) timeout, (5) sequence numbers.

**Cumulative acknowledgment:** `ACK(20)` means every frame with sequence number < 20 has been received correctly, and frame #20 is the next one the receiver expects.

children.title: Socket Programming — TCP/UDP Basics (C / BSD sockets)
children.label: Socket Programming
children.summary: Client-server socket programs share a common structure: create a socket, address it, then either connect (TCP client) / bind+listen+accept (TCP server) before exchanging data.
children.core_idea:
### Roles
- **Client** — initiates a connection; needs the server's IP address and port
- **Server** — waits for connections on a known port; once a client connects, the server has the client's IP + port too

### Creating a Socket
```c
int socket(int domain, int type, int protocol);
```
- `domain` — communication domain, `PF_INET` for IPv4
- `type` — `SOCK_STREAM` for TCP, `SOCK_DGRAM` for UDP
- `protocol` — usually `0` (let the OS pick based on type)
- Returns a socket descriptor (int) on success, `-1` on failure

### Addressing — `struct sockaddr_in`
```c
struct sockaddr_in addr;
addr.sin_family      = PF_INET;
addr.sin_port        = htons(portNum);      // host-to-network byte order
addr.sin_addr.s_addr = inet_addr(ipDest);   // for clients: server's IP
// for servers binding to any local interface: INADDR_ANY
```
- `htons()` converts an integer port to network byte order
- `inet_addr()` converts a dotted-decimal string to a binary IP address

### TCP Flow — Client vs. Server
```
Server:  socket() → bind() → listen() → accept() → read()/write() → close()
Client:  socket() →                    connect()  → write()/read() → close()
```
- `bind(sockfd, addr, addrlen)` — attaches the socket to a specific local port; server-side
- `listen(sockfd, backlog)` — marks the socket as passive, `backlog` sets the max queued pending connections
- `accept()` — blocks until a client connects, returns a *new* socket descriptor for that specific connection
- `connect()` — client-side; initiates the TCP handshake to the server's address

### UDP Difference
UDP has no `listen()`/`accept()`/`connect()` handshake — after `socket()` and `bind()`, both sides just use `sendto()`/`recvfrom()` directly, since there's no persistent connection state.

children.title: Email Security — Architecture, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, and Spoofing Risks
children.label: Email Security
children.summary: SMTP has no built-in sender authentication; SPF, DKIM, and DMARC layer trust on top of it using DNS-published records.
children.core_idea:
### Email Architecture
- **MTA (Message Transfer Agent)** — routes and delivers mail between servers
- **UA (User Agent)** — the client application a user reads/composes mail with

### Why Email Is Inherently Insecure
- **No host-to-host authentication** — SMTP trusts whatever `MAIL FROM:` claims; the sender's IP could be spoofed and the MTA's recorded "sending IP" can't be fully trusted either
- **Clear-text by default** — messages are stored unencrypted on both the MTA and UA, and legacy UAs send login credentials in clear text
- UAs supporting scripting extensions (e.g. VBA macros in Outlook) expand the attack surface for malicious attachments

### SPF (Sender Policy Framework)
A DNS TXT record listing which mail servers are authorized to send mail for a domain. Receivers check the connecting server's IP against this list.

### DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail)
Cryptographically signs outgoing mail with a private key; the public key is published in DNS, letting receivers verify the message wasn't altered in transit and genuinely came from a server holding the domain's private key.

### DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance)
Ties SPF and DKIM together and tells receivers what to do when both fail:
1. Receiver checks the sending IP against the domain's **SPF** record
2. Receiver validates the message signature against the domain's **DKIM** public key
3. Receiver checks **alignment** — does the authenticated SPF/DKIM domain match the visible "From:" domain?
4. If SPF *or* DKIM passes **and** aligns with the visible From domain → DMARC passes
5. If DMARC fails, the receiver acts per the domain's published policy: deliver anyway, quarantine (spam), or reject outright
6. Receivers send the domain owner a daily aggregate report of authentication results across all observed senders — useful for spotting spoofing attempts against your own domain

children.title: Firewalls — Types, Rule Sets & Architecture
children.label: Firewalls
children.summary: Firewalls sit between networks and allow/deny traffic by rule; screening routers do fast coarse filtering, application firewalls do deep but slower inspection, and DMZs isolate exposed services.
children.core_idea:
### What a Firewall Does
Sits between two networks and makes a yes/no forwarding decision per packet based on a rule set. It can inspect a single layer or all layers (application, TCP, IP, network) — the more layers inspected and the more rules defined, the lower the throughput.

### Rule Set Philosophy
- **Default deny** — the default answer to "let this packet through?" is **no**; administrators must explicitly open what's needed
- The application layer is hardest to write rules for since every protocol (email, web, FTP) behaves differently

### Types
| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **Dual-Homed Host** (most common) | Two NICs, each with its own IP/TCP stack; a rule set sits between them and traffic passes through based on it — also called a pass-through firewall |
| **Air Gap Firewall** | Two separate applications on the same interface communicate with each other to relay traffic — more isolated than a standard dual-homed host |
| **Screening Router** | Filters at TCP/IP layer only (IP address, protocol type, port, bad-IP lists) — fast, coarse, often paired in front of a full firewall to shed obviously-bad traffic before deep inspection |

### Attack Vectors Against Firewalls
1. **Break the firewall itself** — exploit a vulnerability in its software/OS
2. **Piggyback on allowed traffic** — e.g. compromise a web server, then tunnel other traffic over the already-open port 80 (commonly via malware placed on that host)

### Firewall Security Considerations
- Application firewalls are often fully functional computers — running extra services (e.g. DNS) on the same box adds risk
- Remote administrative access to the firewall needs strong auth + encryption, and is itself a DoS target
- Misconfiguration is one of the most common real-world firewall vulnerabilities
- Physical security matters as much as the ruleset — an attacker with physical access to the box or its remote-management channel bypasses the rules entirely

### DMZ (Demilitarized Zone)
Layered defense with two firewalls:
```
[Internet] → [Firewall: loose rules] → [DMZ: mail/web/FTP servers] → [Firewall: strict rules] → [Internal Network]
```
Hosts in the DMZ ("sacrificial hosts") are exposed to the internet but isolated from the trusted internal network — paired with logging, IDS, and NAT.

### Proxies
Applications needing real-time transfer (that can't do simple store-and-forward) tunnel through the firewall via a **proxy**, which also centralizes logging: `[Internal net] → [Proxy] → [Firewall: web-only] → [Internet]`.

children.title: Access Control Models — MAC, DAC & RBAC
children.label: Access Control Models
children.summary: Mandatory Access Control compares security labels/clearances; Role-Based Access Control grants permissions through roles rather than individual users, governed by hierarchy, exclusivity, and cardinality constraints.
children.core_idea:
### Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
Access is controlled centrally by comparing a subject's **security clearance** against an object's **security label/classification** (e.g. Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) — the user cannot change these labels themselves. Common in government/military systems.

### Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
The resource *owner* decides who else gets access (e.g. standard Unix file permissions, ACLs) — more flexible than MAC but weaker for enforcing organization-wide policy since any owner can grant access.

### Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
Access is granted through **roles** rather than directly to individual users — a role bundles a set of permissions, and users are assigned to roles. Roles can be static or dynamic (activated per session).

**Constraints that govern role design:**
- **Hierarchy** — a higher-level role automatically includes all access rights of the roles beneath it
- **Mutual exclusivity** — certain roles cannot be held by the same user simultaneously (e.g. "submit expense" and "approve expense")
- **Cardinality** — limits on role assignment, such as:
  - Maximum number of users who may hold a given role
  - Maximum number of roles a single user may be assigned
- **Prerequisite** — a condition that must already be satisfied before a user can be assigned a given role (e.g. must hold Role A before being eligible for Role B)

RBAC scales far better than assigning permissions per-user directly, and is the dominant model in enterprise identity systems.

children.title: Identity & Authentication Fundamentals
children.label: Identity & Authentication Fundamentals
children.summary: Authentication validates a claimed identity across four directions (user↔host, host↔host, user↔user), using some combination of what you know, have, and are.
children.core_idea:
### Identity vs. Authentication
- **Identity** — the characteristics by which a person or thing is recognized
- **Digital Identity** — the electronic representation of a real-world entity participating in electronic transactions; raises questions of privacy, ownership, and security
- **Authentication** — the process of *validating* a claimed identity; the first step of any identity management system

### Four Directions of Authentication
| Type | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **User → Host** | A person proves identity to a system | Logging in (most common case) |
| **Host → Host** | Machine-to-machine identity verification | Historically IP-based (weak — easily spoofed) |
| **User → User** | Verifying identity between two people | Secure email, digital signatures on contracts |
| **Host → User** | A server proves its identity to the user | TLS/HTTPS certificates |

### Three Factors (User → Host)
- **Something you know** — passwords, PINs; most common, limited by human memory and reuse
- **Something you have** — key cards, hardware tokens; convenient, but can be lost or stolen
- **Something you are** — biometrics (fingerprint, voice, retina); hard to fake but raises privacy/scalability concerns and can't be "reset" if compromised

### Failure Categories
**Infrastructure & Trust Model Failures** — authentication systems rely on chains of trust, and expanding that chain expands risk:
- Compromise of a Certificate Authority's private key collapses trust across everything that CA vouches for
- Implicit trust based on network identity (IP address) is inherently spoofable
- Overprivileged service accounts widen the blast radius of any single compromise
- **Mitigation — Zero Trust:** identity-based access control with continuous validation; assume breach at all times rather than trusting anything by network location

**Human & Governance Failures** — technical controls get undermined by policy gaps and social engineering:
| Attack | Description |
|---|---|
| Phishing | Credential harvesting or OAuth token abuse via deceptive messages |
| MFA Fatigue | Bombarding a user with push notifications until they approve one out of frustration |
| Help Desk Social Engineering | Impersonating an executive/user to trigger a fraudulent password reset |

Mitigations: phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/passkeys), strict identity-verification protocols for support staff, ongoing security-awareness training.

children.title: Adversarial Thinking — Motivations, Goals & Insider Threats
children.label: Adversarial Thinking
children.summary: Adversaries pursue a common set of goals (espionage, disruption, resource control) driven by varied motivations, and combine cyber and physical techniques to reach them.
children.core_idea:
### What Is an Adversary?
An individual, group, or entity acting in conflict against another to achieve specific goals, often at the target's expense — operating across physical, cyber, and social domains.

### Crosscutting Goals
Regardless of motivation, adversaries tend to pursue: **espionage** (covert intelligence gathering), **disruption** (degrading systems/operations), **reputation damage**, **resource control** (acquiring or denying access to assets), **social engineering** (manipulating people), and **intimidation/coercion**.

### Motivations
Political, economic, ideological/religious, personal (revenge/grievance), technological (IP theft/disruption), and strategic/military.

### Combining Cyber and Physical
- **Cyber aiding a physical attack** — mapping security protocols and facility layouts, disabling alarms/cameras/access controls before an intrusion, disrupting communications, or manipulating OT (operational technology) to create physical hazards or distractions
- **Physical aiding a cyber attack** — USB drops or device tampering to install malware, plugging directly into a secure network port after gaining building access, or intercepting hardware in the supply chain to implant backdoors
- **Hybrid attacks** coordinate both simultaneously; **supply chain attacks** compromise a trusted third party to reach the real target

### Business Email Compromise (BEC) — Two Entry Points
1. **Inserting into an existing relationship** — compromise a valid email account (password guessing, phishing, malware) and use its legitimacy to manipulate ongoing conversations, or join a video call impersonating a known participant
2. **Starting a new relationship** — a fake email/bank impersonation, a spoofed phone call, or a text message designed to steal credentials or trigger a fraudulent payment; interactive "grooming" often precedes the actual ask

### Insider Threats
- **Intentional** — malicious insiders; risk scales with the number of egress points and protocols available to exfiltrate data
- **Accidental** — data leaks via email/IM/file-sharing simply because systems have become more integrated and easy to (mis)use
- **Intentionally Accidental** — as technical defenses harden, attackers use social engineering against insiders to get them to leak information "by accident"

children.title: Footprinting & Network Reconnaissance Techniques
children.label: Footprinting & Network Reconnaissance
children.summary: Footprinting builds a profile of a target across internet, intranet, and extranet before an attack — using public records, DNS enumeration, and network mapping.
children.core_idea:
### What Is Footprinting?
The process of building a profile of a target before an attack — analogous to casing a building. Targets three areas: **Internet** (domains, addresses, topology), **Intranet** (internal tech, VPNs, remote access), **Extranet** (access controls exposed to partners).

### Techniques
**Website analysis** — mirror the site for offline analysis, gather location/M&A/contact/privacy-policy info (which can hint at security posture), review HTML source for developer comments left behind.

**Newsgroups & social engineering setup** — search for posts from the target's IT staff, and build employee lists via search operators that find pages linking back to the company domain.

**Public databases** — state/local government registries can reveal corporate partnerships or subsidiaries, useful for finding trust relationships to exploit.

**DNS enumeration:**
- `whois` reveals organization info, admin/technical contacts, DNS servers, registrar
- `nslookup`/`dig` resolve hostnames and can reveal record structure
- Zone transfers (if misconfigured) expose the entire domain map in one query

**Network mapping** — traceroute reveals the path (and often internal topology) between attacker and target using the TTL trick; port 53/UDP (DNS) is commonly open when most other UDP ports are filtered, making it a useful probe.

### Attack Categories Once Recon Is Complete
| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Header attacks** | Crafting invalid packets — identical source/destination, illegal reserved bits, out-of-spec field values — to confuse protocol stacks |
| **Protocol attacks** | Instructing a device to stop communicating; for connectionless protocols, spoofing a "server down" response to a client; SYN floods overwhelming a server with incomplete handshakes |
| **Network timing attacks** | Valid packets sent out of order, too fast, or deliberately withheld |
| **Authentication attacks** | Exploiting IP-based trust rather than credential-based authentication |
| **Traffic attacks** | Flooding (single-source or distributed/DDoS), broadcast storms that amplify damage, and sniffing on any layer an attacker can observe |

children.title: ARP & ARP Spoofing — Layer 2 MITM
children.label: ARP & ARP Spoofing
children.summary: ARP resolves IP addresses to MAC addresses with no authentication; forged ARP replies let an attacker poison a victim's cache and sit in the middle of local traffic.
children.core_idea:
### How ARP Works
Address Resolution Protocol maps a known IP address to the MAC address needed to actually deliver a frame on the local segment. A host broadcasts "who has IP X?" and the owner replies with its MAC — the requester caches the mapping.

### ARP Spoofing (Cache Poisoning)
ARP has **no authentication** — any host can claim to own any IP address. An attacker sends forged ("gratuitous") ARP replies claiming to own the gateway's (or another host's) IP, poisoning victims' ARP caches so their traffic routes through the attacker instead — a classic Layer 2 man-in-the-middle.
- Attackers periodically re-send gratuitous ARP to keep the poisoned entry from expiring back to the correct mapping

### Defense
- **Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)** on managed switches, validating ARP packets against a trusted binding table (often built from DHCP snooping)
- **Static ARP entries** for critical infrastructure like default gateways
- Encryption above Layer 2 (TLS, etc.) limits the *value* of a successful MITM even if ARP poisoning succeeds

children.title: VLAN Hopping
children.label: VLAN Hopping
children.summary: Double-tagging or switch spoofing tricks a switch into forwarding frames into a VLAN the attacker shouldn't have access to.
children.core_idea:
### Double Tagging
An attacker on the native VLAN sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags. The first switch strips the outer tag (matching the native VLAN) and forwards the frame — the inner tag then gets treated as if it were the original, hopping the frame into a different VLAN than the attacker's actual port.

### Switch Spoofing
If a port is left in dynamic trunking mode, an attacker's host can negotiate a trunk link with the switch (mimicking a legitimate switch), gaining access to all VLANs carried on that trunk.

### Mitigations
- Explicitly configure trunk ports rather than relying on auto-negotiation
- Disable DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) on access ports
- Never use VLAN 1 (the default native VLAN) for user traffic, and ensure native VLAN configuration matches on both ends of a trunk
- Keep the management VLAN separate from user VLANs entirely

children.title: iptables — Stateful Filtering
children.label: iptables
children.summary: Stateful firewalls track connection state (conntrack) so return traffic for an established connection is allowed without opening inbound ports broadly.
children.core_idea:
### Stateful vs. Stateless
A stateless firewall must evaluate every packet against the rule set independently. A stateful firewall tracks connections in a **conntrack table** and can allow return traffic for a connection it has already approved, without a separate inbound rule.

```
iptables -A INPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
iptables -P INPUT DROP
```

### Best Practice Pattern
- **Default-drop** the INPUT chain, then explicitly allow only what's needed
- Allow `ESTABLISHED,RELATED` traffic first so replies to outbound/approved connections aren't re-evaluated from scratch
- Log dropped packets sparingly — verbose logging on a high-drop-rate firewall can itself become a DoS vector (log flooding filling disk/CPU)

commands.explain: Allow return traffic for connections already approved, without opening new inbound ports.
Set the default policy to deny — an explicit-allow model.

children.title: Wireshark — Display Filters
children.label: Wireshark
children.summary: Display filters narrow the packet list after capture; the syntax is Wireshark-specific and differs from BPF capture filters.
children.core_idea:
### Display vs. Capture Filters
- **Capture filters** (BPF syntax, e.g. `tcpdump`-style) decide what gets recorded in the first place
- **Display filters** (Wireshark's own syntax) narrow what's shown from an already-captured file — nothing is discarded, so you can always broaden the filter later

### Common Filters
| Filter | Matches |
|---|---|
| `ip.addr == 10.0.0.5` | Traffic to/from an IP |
| `tcp.port == 443` | Traffic on a specific port |
| `http.request` | HTTP request packets only |
| `tls.handshake.type == 1` | TLS ClientHello packets |

Combine filters with `&&` and `||`. Right-click a TCP packet → **Follow → TCP Stream** to reconstruct the full application-layer conversation in one view — invaluable for reading plaintext protocols or reassembling a file transfer.

children.title: DNS Zone Transfer (AXFR) — Exposure Risk
children.label: DNS Zone Transfer
children.summary: An unrestricted AXFR request dumps an entire DNS zone in one query, exposing internal hostnames and network layout that would otherwise take extensive scanning to enumerate.
children.core_idea:
Zone transfers are meant to replicate a DNS zone from a primary server to its secondaries — a legitimate, expected operation between trusted servers. If an authoritative server allows AXFR requests from *any* client, though, an attacker gets the entire zone file in one shot: every subdomain, internal-facing hostname, and inferred network layout.

```
dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com
```

**Mitigation:** explicitly restrict transfers with an `allow-transfer` ACL naming only legitimate secondary servers (e.g. in BIND's zone configuration) — the default should never be "allow from anywhere."

children.title: OverTheWire Bandit — CLI Skills Reference (Levels 0–14)
children.label: OverTheWire Bandit
children.summary: The Bandit wargame teaches core Linux CLI skills through 14 escalating levels — filename edge cases, hidden files, encoding, compression, and SSH key auth.
children.core_idea:
Each level's password unlocks SSH access to the next. Connect with:
```
ssh banditN@bandit.labs.overthewire.org -p 2220
```

| Level | Skill Tested | Key Command(s) |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Basic SSH + reading a file | `ssh bandit0@bandit.labs.overthewire.org -p 2220` → `cat readme` |
| **1** | Filename starting with `-` is parsed as a flag, not a name | `cat ./-` (the `./` prefix forces it to be read as a path) |
| **2** | Filenames with spaces | `cat "spaces in this filename"` (or escape each space: `cat spaces\ in\ this\ filename`) |
| **3** | Hidden files (dotfiles) don't show in plain `ls` | `ls -la` reveals them; `cat ...Hiding-From-You` |
| **4** | Distinguishing file types when names are unhelpful | `file ./-*` to identify which of many candidate files is actually ASCII text, then `cat` that one |
| **5** | Finding a file by exact size + readability | `find . -size 1033c` scoped under the target directory, or `du -b -a \| grep 1033` |
| **6** | Finding a file by owner, group, and size across the whole filesystem | `find / -user bandit7 -group bandit6 -size 33c 2>/dev/null` |
| **7** | Extracting a value next to a known keyword | `grep "millionth" data.txt` |
| **8** | Finding the one non-duplicate line in a large file | `sort data.txt \| uniq -u` (uniq only detects adjacent duplicates, so sorting first is required) |
| **9** | Pulling human-readable text out of a binary/mixed file | `strings data.txt \| grep "==="` |
| **10** | Decoding Base64 | `base64 -d data.txt` |
| **11** | Reversing ROT13 | `tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m' < data.txt` |
| **12** | Unwrapping multiple layers of hex-encoding + compression | `xxd -r` to convert a hexdump back to binary, then repeatedly `file` the result to identify each layer (gzip/bzip2/tar/etc.) and unwrap with the matching tool until you reach plain ASCII |
| **13** | SSH login using a provided private key | `ssh -i sshkey.private -p 2220 bandit14@bandit.labs.overthewire.org` (chmod the key to `600` first if SSH refuses it for being too open) |

### Recurring Techniques Across All Levels
- **File identification when extensions lie or are missing:** `file <name>` — never trust an extension, always verify actual file type before choosing a tool
- **Unwrapping nested encodings:** work outside-in — identify the current layer with `file`, strip it with the matching tool (`base64 -d`, `xxd -r`, `gzip -d`, `bzip2 -d`, `tar -xf`), then re-check with `file` and repeat until you hit plain text
- **`find` for targeted filesystem search** by owner (`-user`), group (`-group`), exact size (`-size Nc`), or type — far more precise than manually browsing directories
- **`grep`/`sort`/`uniq`/`strings`/`tr`** form the core text-processing toolkit for pulling a specific value out of a large or obfuscated file

children.title: Software-Based Fault Tolerance on COTS Hardware
children.label: Software
children.summary: Fault tolerance is traditionally handled by specialized hardware; software-based techniques like arithmetic coding let commercial off-the-shelf hardware detect faults instead.
children.core_idea:
### The Problem
Hardware unreliability is a growing concern as systems push commodity hardware harder. Faults are classified by duration:
- **Transient faults** — occur briefly, then disappear (e.g. a cosmic-ray-induced bit flip)
- **Permanent faults** — continuously affect the system once they occur (physical hardware damage)
- **Intermittent faults** — occur briefly but recur periodically, often signaling a developing hardware issue before it becomes permanent

### Traditional Approach vs. Software-Based Alternative
Fault tolerance has traditionally been handled by **specialized, redundant hardware** — and is a hard requirement for safety-critical systems under standards like **IEC 61508**. Specialized fault-tolerant hardware is expensive, though, which motivates research into **software-based fault tolerance** techniques that let commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware achieve comparable fault detection without custom silicon.

**Arithmetic coding** is one such technique — encoding integer calculations in a way that makes corruption from a fault detectable in the result itself, trading some computational overhead for fault-detection capability without needing specialized hardware. The core research tradeoff is exactly that: **detection capability vs. performance overhead** — stronger encoding catches more fault classes but costs more cycles per operation.

children.title: Safety-Critical Hazard Analysis — Case Studies
children.label: Safety
children.summary: Fault Tree Analysis and static code analysis applied to real safety-critical systems (radiosurgery devices, Mars lander software) reveal single-point failure paths before they reach production.
children.core_idea:
Systematic hazard and failure analysis — using **Fault Tree Analysis**, **SFMECA** (Software Failure Mode, Effects, and Criticality Analysis), and formal verification — applied to two illustrative safety-critical domains:

- **Stereotactic radiosurgery devices** — medical systems where a software fault translates directly into patient harm; fault trees here identify **single-point failure paths** (any one component whose failure alone causes the hazard) and derive **minimal cut sets** (the smallest combinations of component failures that together trigger the top-level hazard)
- **Mars lander software** (referencing the well-documented Mars Polar Lander loss) — static code analysis applied to flight software to detect latent defects before launch, since safety-critical embedded software often can't be patched once deployed

**Why this matters for security, not just safety:** the same fault-tree and static-analysis methodology used to find *accidental* failure paths is directly applicable to finding *deliberately exploitable* ones — a single point of failure an engineer worries about for reliability is often the same weak point an attacker would target for disruption.

children.title: Web Fundamentals — URLs, CGI & Apache Access Control
children.label: Web Fundamentals
children.summary: HTTP is a stateless file-transport protocol; server security lives largely in access-control config (.htaccess, httpd.conf) and how CGI/user input is handled.
children.core_idea:
### Request Flow
A user request travels: browser → web server → (if dynamic) application server → database, with the response following back the same path. HTTP is fundamentally a **stateless file transport protocol** — the browser interprets returned files (HTML, images, scripts) to render the page; state (login, sessions) is bolted on top via cookies.

### URL Structure
```
scheme://[user:password]@hostname:[port]/path
```
- Default web port: **80**; secure (TLS) port: **443**
- Same scheme structure used for HTTP and FTP

### Server Directory Structure
| Directory | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `cgi-bin` | Default location for CGI executables |
| `conf` | Configuration files, read at startup |
| `html` | Document root — served content |
| `logs` | Access/error/agent/referer logs |

### Key `httpd.conf` Directives
- **User / Group** — UID/GID the server runs as
- **DocumentRoot** — where files are served from when no path is given
- **UserDir** — per-user web directory (`/~user`)
- **AccessFileName** — usually `.htaccess`; enables per-directory login rules
- **Alias** — serves content from outside DocumentRoot (safer than symlinks)
- **ScriptAlias** — alternate directory for CGI scripts
- **IndexIgnore** — hides specific files from directory listings

### CGI (Common Gateway Interface)
Lets server-side programs process browser input and output HTML. **Any time user input drives a server-side program, that's a security risk** — CGI scripts need rigorous input validation. `cgi-bin` should live outside the document tree, and administrators typically don't allow users to create their own CGI scripts.

**Classic example:** a "finger" CGI script that looked up logged-in users. An attacker submitted `nobody; /bin/cat /etc/passwd` — the shell treated the semicolon as a command separator and dumped the password file to the page.

### Access Control (`.htaccess`)
```
AuthUserFile  /etc/pw1
AuthGroupFile /etc/grp
AuthType  Basic
AuthName  Example1
<Limit Get>
  Require valid-user
</Limit>
```
- Rules can restrict by **User**, **Group**, or **Host/IP**, and combine with `order deny,allow` / `order allow,deny` chains
- **Never place password/group files inside the document tree** — anyone could read them over HTTP; keep them in `conf` or `/etc`
- Basic Auth passwords are no more secure than standard UNIX passwords — the same cracking tools apply
- `htpasswd -c passwordfile username` creates/updates the password file (omit `-c` after the first time); anyone with write access to that file's directory can tamper with it

### Directory & Global Options
- **ExecCGI** / **Indexes** / **Includes** — per-directory toggles (Includes is usually disabled — security risk)
- **AllowOverride** in the global config must be granted before per-directory `.htaccess` overrides take effect at all

### CMS Note
Most modern sites run atop a CMS (WordPress, Drupal) with its own authentication layer — convenient, but third-party plugins are a major expansion of attack surface.

children.title: Web Server & Application Attack Categories
children.label: Web Server & Application
children.summary: Web attacks span server-executable bugs, CGI/input-validation flaws, and application-layer issues like SQLi, XSS, and stateless-session abuse via cookies.
children.core_idea:
### OWASP Top Ten
The industry-standard reference for the most critical web application risks (owasp.org/www-project-top-ten) — used as a coverage checklist during assessments, not an exhaustive list.

### Web Server Attack Categories
1. **Server executable vulnerabilities** — bugs in the server software itself
2. **Sample/default files** — shipped with server distributions; may include debug pages or file-upload demos left enabled
3. **Source code disclosure** — misconfigurations exposing server-side source instead of executing it
4. **Canonicalization attacks** — manipulating path format (e.g. `../text.html` where `c:\text.html` was expected) to escape the intended directory
5. **Server extension bugs** — vulnerabilities in add-ons like PHP or SSL modules
6. **Input validation attacks** — buffer overflows in CGI/backend code, and injection attacks

Scanners like **Nikto** and **Whisker** automate detection of these categories against a live server.

### Web Application Attacks
- **Crawling/downloading** a site (Wget, Offline Explorer Pro) to map attack surface offline; search-engine dorking (`"index of /password"`) to find exposed files directly
- **Assessment areas**: authentication, session management, database interaction, generic input validation
- **SQL Injection** — unsanitized input reaches a raw SQL query; impact depends on the backend and how permissively it's configured
- **Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)** — malicious script posted to a shared surface (e.g. a message board) executes in *other* users' browsers when they view it

### Cookies & Statelessness
HTTP is stateless, so cookies carry session state across requests. Early cookie implementations let any site read another site's cookies; the same-origin restriction (only the originating site can read its own cookie) came later as a fix. Passwords are sometimes still stored in clear text inside cookies by poorly-built apps — never assume a cookie's contents are opaque or safe.
- **Session cookies** — expire when the browser closes
- **Persistent cookies** — survive across sessions, commonly used for tracking

### SSL / TLS
Sits between HTTP and TCP to provide an encrypted channel (**port 443**); the browser ships with a trust store of certificate authorities to validate server certificates.

### Server Logs
| Log | Contents |
|---|---|
| Access log | Every file transferred — `machine user auth-data time "command"` |
| Referer log | Which page linked to this request |
| Agent log | Client browser/user-agent string |
| Error log | Requests for files that don't exist |

### Web Application Firewalls (WAF)
Sit in front of the application to monitor, filter, and block malicious traffic (e.g. **WordFence** for WordPress) — complements, but doesn't replace, fixing the underlying vulnerability.

children.title: Client-Side Web Attack Techniques
children.label: Client
children.summary: Client-side attacks target the browser and user directly — manipulating rendered content, hijacking sessions, or abusing trust the user places in the page.
children.core_idea:
| Attack | How It Works |
|---|---|
| **Man-in-the-Browser (MitB)** | Malware infects the browser itself and silently modifies transactions (e.g. altering bank transfer details) without the user noticing |
| **Session Hijacking / Cookie Stealing** | Attacker captures a session cookie (easier over plain HTTP or with insecure cookie flags) to impersonate the logged-in user |
| **Clickjacking** | A transparent iframe is layered over a legitimate-looking page; the user's click actually hits a hidden element on another page (e.g. granting camera access, changing a privacy setting). Defense: **CSP `frame-ancestors`** and the **`X-Frame-Options`** header |
| **SSL Stripping** | Attacker downgrades what should be an HTTPS connection to plain HTTP, intercepting data in transit |
| **DNS Spoofing / Cache Poisoning** | Forged DNS responses redirect the victim to a malicious site instead of the real one |
| **Watering Hole Attack** | Compromise a site the target group visits often, infecting their browsers when they visit as usual |
| **Malvertising** | Malicious code injected into ad content — infects visitors passively, with no download required |
| **Web-Based Cryptojacking** | A mining script (historically CoinHive) runs in the visitor's browser, consuming their CPU to mine cryptocurrency for the attacker |
| **Browser Fingerprinting** | Tracks users via a combination of OS, browser version, fonts, and screen configuration — works without cookies or explicit consent |
| **Browser Lock / Tech Support Scams** | A page traps the browser (repeated pop-ups, fake full-screen "infected" warnings) to scare the victim into calling a fraudulent support number and paying |
| **LFI / RFI (Local/Remote File Inclusion)** | Attacker gets the server to include an attacker-chosen local (LFI) or remote (RFI) file, leading to information disclosure or code execution |
| **WebRTC Leaks** | A browser bug reveals the user's real IP address even while behind a VPN |
| **Zero-Day Browser Exploits** | Attacks against browser vulnerabilities with no patch yet available |

### Web / User Tracking (adjacent, not always malicious)
- **Web beacons / tracking pixels** — invisible 1×1 images that phone home on load, reporting view time/engagement; widely used in email and ad tracking (e.g. Facebook Pixel)
- **Behavioral tracking & retargeting** — ad networks correlate browsing history to serve targeted ads; combined with location data (IP/GPS/Wi-Fi) and persistent mobile ad identifiers (IDFA, Google Advertising ID)

children.label: Application & Freeware Firewalls
children.summary: Application firewalls are built into the software they protect (WAFs being the most common); freeware firewalls range from router-embedded to OS-level personal firewalls.
children.core_idea:
### Application Firewalls
Integrated directly into an application rather than sitting in front of it as a separate device. The most common case is the **Web Application Firewall (WAF)** — inspects HTTP traffic at the application layer for attack patterns (SQLi, XSS payloads, etc.) that a network-layer firewall can't see.

### Freeware / Consumer Firewalls
| Firewall | Where It Runs |
|---|---|
| Built-in router firewall | Most home access/routers |
| **pfSense** / **OPNsense** | Dedicated open-source firewall distributions |
| **ZoneAlarm** and similar | Personal, OS-level firewall software |

Most desktop/mobile OSes also ship a built-in personal firewall as a baseline — freeware/open-source options generally add more granular rule control and logging than the OS default.

children.title: SQL Injection — UNION-Based
children.label: SQL Injection
children.summary: ### Mechanism When user input is concatenated directly into a SQL query, `UNION SELECT` lets an attacker append an entirely separate query whose results get merged into the original output.
children.core_idea:
### Mechanism
When user input is concatenated directly into a SQL query, `UNION SELECT` lets an attacker append an entirely separate query whose results get merged into the original output.

### Typical Workflow
1. **Find the column count** — `ORDER BY n` (increment `n` until it errors) or `UNION SELECT null,null,...` until the column count matches
2. **Extract schema** — once columns align, query `information_schema.tables` / `.columns` to enumerate database structure
3. **Extract data** — substitute real column names/tables into the UNION query to pull sensitive data directly into the page output

### Fix
Use **prepared statements / parameterized queries** everywhere, or an ORM's parameter binding — never string-concatenate user input into SQL.

children.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
children.label: Cross
children.summary: Reflected XSS executes in the victim's browser from a crafted URL; stored XSS persists in server-side data (comments, profiles) and hits every future viewer.
children.core_idea:
### Types
- **Reflected** — the payload is part of the request (e.g. a query parameter) and gets echoed back into the response unescaped; requires tricking the victim into clicking a crafted link
- **Stored** — the payload is saved server-side (a comment, profile field, etc.) and executes for every user who later views that content — no crafted link needed
- **DOM-based** — client-side JavaScript writes untrusted input directly into the DOM; the payload never even touches the server, so server-side sanitization alone won't catch it

### Defense
- **Context-aware output encoding** — encode differently depending on whether output lands in HTML body, an attribute, a URL, or a `<script>` block
- **Content Security Policy (CSP)** — restricts which script sources the browser will execute
- **HttpOnly** flag on session cookies — prevents JavaScript (including injected XSS payloads) from reading them, limiting the payoff of a successful XSS

children.title: CSRF — Token & SameSite Defenses
children.label: CSRF
children.summary: CSRF tricks a logged-in browser into submitting unwanted state-changing requests. Synchronizer tokens and SameSite cookies mitigate it.
children.core_idea:
### Mechanism
A victim is logged into a site; a malicious page (or email/link) triggers a request to that site — the browser automatically attaches the victim's session cookie, so the request looks legitimate to the server even though the victim never intended to send it.

### Defenses
- **Anti-CSRF tokens** — an unpredictable, per-session token embedded in forms; the server rejects state-changing requests that don't include the correct token
- **SameSite cookies** — `SameSite=Lax` or `Strict` stops the browser from attaching the cookie to most cross-origin requests in the first place
- **Origin/Referer verification** — an extra check on sensitive POST requests, confirming the request actually originated from your own site

children.title: OWASP Top 10 — Priority Web Risks
children.label: OWASP Top 10
children.summary: Broken access control and injection consistently rank highest — map findings to Top 10 for stakeholder communication.
children.core_idea: Use the OWASP Top 10 as a **coverage checklist** during assessments and a common vocabulary for communicating findings to stakeholders — not as an exhaustive risk list on its own. For depth beyond the Top 10's headline categories, pair it with the **OWASP ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard)**, which breaks each category into specific, testable requirements.

children.core_idea:
A useful mental model for data loss prevention conversations:
- Data makes up the bulk of what an organization actually *is*, the way water makes up most of the earth's surface
- Data is **hard to hold onto once it leaves its container** — once it's copied to an email, a USB drive, or a personal device, pulling it back is often impossible
- People are often **willing to share data when asked**, especially by someone who sounds authoritative or trusted — the same dynamic that makes social engineering effective
- The key place the analogy breaks down: **data can be copied** infinitely without depleting the original, unlike water — meaning a single leak doesn't just relocate the asset, it multiplies it
