children.title: Legal Issues in Cybersecurity — Criminal vs. Civil Law
children.label: Legal Issues in Cybersecurity
children.summary: Criminal cybercrime cases need proof beyond a reasonable doubt; civil cases need only a preponderance of evidence — and cross-border jurisdiction complicates both.
children.core_idea:
### Criminal vs. Civil Law
| | Criminal Law | Civil Law |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard of proof** | Beyond a reasonable doubt | Preponderance of evidence (>50%) |
| **Typical use** | Prosecuting cybercrime directly | IP disputes, defamation, harassment |
| **Challenge** | Juries often struggle with technical detail, making prosecution harder despite newer, clearer statutes | Setting damages for a purely digital harm is difficult |

### Key Legal Challenges
- **Unauthorized access laws** are often ambiguously worded and hard to prosecute cleanly
- **Damages in civil cases** are hard to quantify when the harm is data exposure or downtime rather than a physical loss
- Software vendors have historically avoided liability for security bugs in their products, though this is shifting as breach severity increases
- **International jurisdiction** is one of the biggest practical obstacles — laws differ sharply across borders, and attribution (proving *who* did it, in a court-admissible way) is difficult even when the technical evidence is clear

### Types of Protected Information
Copyright, unauthorized-access statutes, theft laws, and domain-specific regulation (e.g. **HIPAA** for medical information) each carry their own legal framework and evidentiary standard — an investigator needs to know which regime applies before evidence collection even begins.

children.title: Forensic Tool Validation & the "Black Box" Defense
children.label: Forensic Tool Validation &
children.summary: Digital forensic tools must be validated, not trusted blindly — the Daubert standard requires scientific evidence to come from methods with a known, tested error rate.
children.core_idea:
### Why Validation Matters
The core premise of any digital investigation is **trusting the tools you use** — and in court, that trust gets tested directly. The U.S. **Daubert standard** requires scientific evidence to be derived from methods that are reliable and have a known, testable error rate. For digital forensics, that means knowing *how often, and in what circumstances*, your tool gets it wrong — not just assuming a well-known or expensive tool is infallible.

Large agencies can lean on NIST's **CFTT (Computer Forensics Tool Testing)** program, but its reports often test outdated versions or configurations that don't match what a smaller lab or student actually runs — and **SWGDE guidance** stresses that validation isn't a one-time checkbox but something that must be repeated as tools and cases evolve.

### Case Study — Validating Autopsy (v4.22.1 / Sleuth Kit)
A controlled experiment built a clean, known-content dataset (a wiped 2GB NTFS virtual disk, 25 documents + 30 images, plus files deliberately removed via Shift+Delete) to test three properties: does the tool find files that are actually present, is the extracted metadata accurate, and are results **repeatable** run to run.

**Results:**
- **100% accuracy** recovering allocated (still-present) files, with bit-for-bit accurate MFT parsing
- **~80% accuracy** recovering deliberately deleted files — failures traced to file-system behavior (data already overwritten), not a flaw specific to the tool. Any tool, commercial or open-source, would hit the same wall once the underlying disk sectors are gone
- **Timezone display bugs** — UTC conversion errors that could shift a displayed timestamp by hours, which is exactly the kind of error that can quietly break an alibi timeline if never validated
- **System files vanished completely on deletion** while user-created files often left recoverable metadata traces — a filesystem-behavior distinction worth knowing before concluding a tool "failed" to find something

### The NTFS Deletion Mechanics Behind This
Every file has an entry in the **MFT (Master File Table)**. Deleting a file does one of two things:
- **Flagging** — marks the MFT entry "Unallocated" (metadata may persist even though it's logically deleted)
- **Bitmap update** — marks the underlying disk space "Free," making it eligible to be overwritten by new data

The dangerous case for an investigator: the MFT entry still shows the file as present, but the underlying data has already been overwritten by something else — metadata says "here," content says "gone." Recognizing this gap is exactly what separates a careful examiner from one who blindly trusts a file listing.

### The "Black Box" Defense
Defense attorneys commonly challenge digital evidence by questioning whether the extraction tool itself was ever validated (the "black box" problem — nobody outside the vendor really knows how it behaves internally). An examiner who has **already measured** their tool's error rate in exactly this kind of scenario can testify: *"I know this tool has a known error rate under Shift+Delete conditions, so I manually verified the file's hex header rather than trusting the tool's report alone."* That turns a known tool limitation into evidence of the examiner's own thoroughness — rather than a gap the defense can exploit.

### Open Source vs. Commercial Reliability
The experiment's core finding pushes back on the assumption that open-source tools are inherently less trustworthy than commercial ones — Autopsy's parsing was bit-for-bit accurate wherever the underlying data still existed; its failures were filesystem-behavior failures any tool would share, not a knock against open-source tooling specifically.

### Lightweight Validation Protocol for Small Labs
1. **Golden image** — maintain a known-content reference dataset (e.g. a reference USB/VHD) and never alter it
2. **Periodic check** — re-run the current tool version against the golden image on a set cadence (e.g. quarterly)
3. **Hash verification** — confirm the tool reproduces the exact known hashes for the golden image's contents
4. **Document deviations** — if a tool update changes behavior (e.g. how timestamps display), log it explicitly as a "Tool Limitation" rather than letting it surface unexpectedly in a live case

**Bottom line:** trust the tool, but verify the data — especially anywhere the case depends on deleted-file recovery or precise timestamps.

children.title: Chain of Custody
children.label: Chain of Custody
children.summary: Every handoff of evidence must be documented with who, when, and why — any undocumented gap can jeopardize admissibility in court.
children.core_idea:
### Core Requirement
Document **who** handled a piece of evidence, **when**, and **why**, at every single transfer — from initial acquisition through to presentation in court. Any undocumented break in that chain gives opposing counsel grounds to challenge the evidence's integrity, regardless of how technically sound the underlying analysis was.

### Practical Controls
- **Write blockers** — hardware devices that physically prevent any write operation to the source disk during acquisition, guaranteeing the original media is never modified
- **Cryptographic hashing on acquisition** (SHA-256) — hash the source immediately upon imaging, and re-verify that hash at every subsequent step to prove the data hasn't changed
- **Work on copies, never the master** — store the original acquired image read-only, and perform all analysis on a working copy, so the master remains available as an unimpeachable reference if anything is ever questioned

commands.explain: Hash a disk image immediately after acquisition to establish an integrity baseline.

children.title: Memory Forensics — Volatility Basics
children.label: Memory Forensics
children.summary: RAM captures reveal running processes, live network connections, and in-memory malware that never touches disk — but only if the analysis profile matches the source kernel.
children.core_idea:
### Why Memory Matters
A disk image alone misses anything that only ever existed in memory — active network connections, decrypted keys held in process memory, and **fileless malware** that runs entirely in RAM without ever writing itself to disk.

### Key Requirement
The analysis **profile must match the source system's kernel** exactly — Volatility (and similar tools) rely on kernel-specific memory-structure offsets to interpret a raw memory dump correctly; a mismatched profile produces garbage or missed artifacts, not just a warning.

### What to Hunt For
- **Injected code** — legitimate processes with foreign code mapped into their address space
- **Process hollowing** — a legitimate process is emptied out and replaced with malicious code while keeping the original process's name/PID, evading naive process-listing checks
- **Command lines in `_EPROCESS`** — the Windows kernel process structure retains the original invocation command line, often revealing exactly how a malicious process was launched even after the fact

children.title: Disk Imaging with dd / dc3dd
children.label: Disk Imaging with dd
children.summary: A forensically sound disk image is a verified bit-for-bit copy, acquired through a hardware write blocker, with every detail of the acquisition logged.
children.core_idea:
### Acquisition
```
dc3dd if=/dev/sdX of=evidence.img hash=sha256 log=acquisition.log
```
`dc3dd` (a forensics-oriented fork of `dd`) adds built-in hashing and logging that plain `dd` lacks — both important for chain-of-custody documentation.

### Requirements for a Sound Acquisition
- **Hardware write blocker** — always, no exceptions; a purely software-based write-blocking approach is a much weaker guarantee under scrutiny
- **Verify with a hash** before any analysis begins — confirm the image matches the source, and re-verify against that same hash at every later step
- **Record serial numbers and tool versions** in the case notes — down to the exact drive serial and imaging software version, since this level of detail is exactly what a validation challenge (see the "Black Box" defense) will probe first

commands.explain: Create a forensic disk image with built-in hashing and an acquisition log.
Plain dd bit-for-bit copy with progress reporting — hash separately before/after if using this instead of dc3dd.

children.title: UNIX Logging Fundamentals — last/utmp/wtmp, syslog & Rootkit Targets
children.label: UNIX Logging Fundamentals
children.summary: Core UNIX log sources (wtmp, syslog, sulog, process accounting) are also the first places a rootkit tampers with — logging and anti-forensics are opposite sides of the same file set.
children.core_idea:
### Three Levels of Intrusion Detection Maturity
1. **Log files** — basic review of what's already recorded
2. **Basic intrusion detection** — actively monitoring events beyond passive log review
3. **Full stateful detection** — comprehensive, real-time analysis across the environment

### Core UNIX Log Files
| Log | Contents | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `last` (log) | Last login time and source machine per user, lives in the home directory | Format differs across UNIX variants |
| `utmp` | Who is **currently** logged in | Not always cleaned up properly by programs — can be unreliable |
| `wtmp` | Login/logout history | The `last` command reads this file |

**All three are trivially modifiable by an attacker with root** — none of them should be treated as tamper-evident on their own.

### Login Scripts as an Attack Vector
Scripts that auto-run at login (`.login`, `.cshrc`) can be modified to execute attacker commands the moment a legitimate user logs in — e.g. silently emailing a file out **before** the attacker even loads a rootkit, exfiltrating data via a channel that looks like normal user activity.

### Syslog
Originally built for sendmail, now the general-purpose UNIX logging facility. **`syslogd`** listens on three sources:
- `/dev/log` — local application messages
- `/dev/klog` — kernel messages
- **UDP port 514** — remote syslog messages from other hosts

Configured via **`syslog.conf`**, which maps a **selector** (facility + severity) to an **action** (where to send the matching events).

**Facilities:** `kern`, `user`, `mail`, `auth` (login/su/anything requiring authentication), `lpt`, `daemon`, `cron`, `news`, `mark` (timestamp), `local0`–`local8` (custom), `syslog`, `ftp`.

**Severity levels (highest → lowest):** `emerg` (system about to crash, usually kernel-sent) → `alert` → `crit` → `err` → `warning` → `notice` (e.g. a user ran `su`) → `info` → `debug` (very verbose, rarely enabled).

```
*.err; kern.debug; auth.notice   /dev/console
*.alert                          root
auth.notice                      @logger.xyz.com
```
Destinations can be a local file, the console, a specific user, a remote log server, or piped through a filter for keyword matching. Every syslog entry carries a timestamp, facility, and the process that generated it.

### Other Notable Log/Monitoring Sources
| Source | Notes |
|---|---|
| **sulog** | Logs every `su` attempt and whether it succeeded — **one of the first files a rootkit modifies** |
| **cron** | Writes to syslog whenever it launches a scheduled job |
| **sendmail** | Can log every message in/out — real privacy implications if enabled broadly |
| **FTP log** | `-l` logs who connected; `-l -l` logs *all* activity (can get overwhelming fast) |
| **`.history`** | Shell history — commonly the first thing an attacker deletes on the way out |
| **Process accounting** | Logs every command any user ran and its runtime; extremely thorough but can fill a disk within days |
| **`ps` output** | Frequently logged for auditing — but `ps` itself is a classic rootkit replacement target, so a compromised host's own `ps` output can't be trusted |
| **`find -mtime <days>`** | Surfaces recently modified files — useful for spotting unexpected changes under `/bin` |

### Log Analysis Tools
- **Tripwire** — computes MD5 hashes of binaries to detect tampering; typically run via cron against `/bin` to catch replaced system binaries
- **Swatch** — real-time log filtering/alerting based on pattern matches

children.title: IDS Functional Components — Sources, Analysis & Response
children.label: IDS Functional Components
children.summary: Every IDS answers three questions: where is it watching (information sources), how does it decide something's wrong (analysis method), and what happens next (response).
children.core_idea:
### 1. Information Sources — Where Is It Monitoring?
Host, network, or application layer — each sees a different slice of activity (see the architecture comparison below).

### 2. Analysis — Is This an Intrusion?
| Method | How It Works |
|---|---|
| **Misuse detection** (signature-based) | Matches traffic against known attack patterns |
| **Virus detection** | Matches against known malware signatures specifically |
| **Anomaly detection** | Flags behavior that deviates from an established normal-use baseline |

### 3. Response — What Happens After Detection?
- **Active response** — an automated action: reconfiguring a firewall on the fly, blocking a scanning IP, or (rarely, and legally fraught) attacking back
- **Passive response** — alarms, notifications, logs, and reports — no automated intervention

### IDS Management Architectures
| Architecture | Description | Drawback |
|---|---|---|
| **Centralized** | One console controls N monitors | Doesn't scale well |
| **Partially Distributed** | N consoles, M monitors, one main console — local processing, major alerts escalate up | Balances scale vs. visibility |
| **Distributed** | Consoles operate independently, no cross-console interaction | Can't recognize a coordinated, system-wide attack from any single console's view |

Also consider placement: **outside** the perimeter (sees raw internet-facing attack attempts) vs. **inside** (sees what actually made it through).

### Timing
- **Interval-based** — periodic polling of collection points; typical for host-based IDS
- **Real-time** — continuous; typical for network-based IDS, where traffic can't be "caught up on" later

children.title: IDS Deployment Types — Network, Host & Application-Based
children.label: IDS Deployment Types
children.summary: Network IDS sees broad traffic but can't inspect encrypted payloads; host IDS sees deep detail but only on one machine and is vulnerable to being disabled by whoever owns that machine.
children.core_idea:
### Network-Based IDS
Essentially a **packet sniffer** deployed at a strategic network point.

**Advantages:** few monitors needed (sometimes just one), minimal network impact, typically runs on a separate/out-of-band management network, and is inherently secure since the sensor itself usually runs no other services.

**Disadvantages:** traffic volume can overwhelm it; some attacks only become visible across *multiple* packets; packets arrive at line speed, making it hard to keep up; **switched networks** don't naturally share traffic to a single point; **encrypted traffic** can't be inspected at all; it can't confirm whether an observed attack actually *succeeded*; and **fragmentation-based evasion** works well against it.

**Switched-network workaround:** a hub/tap inserted between switches, a **mirrored/SPAN port** configured on the switch, or a **dual-port IDS** — traffic between hosts on different switches can also be captured via a tap on the inter-switch uplink.

### Host-Based IDS
Runs directly on the monitored host, drawing from system logs and OS-level activity.

**Advantages:** sees host-level detail invisible to the network, works fine against **encrypted** traffic (it inspects post-decryption), unaffected by switching, and can detect **Trojans** that a network sensor would never see.

**Disadvantages:** management overhead scales with host count; since the **user owns the machine**, they can disable the IDS entirely; it's blind to **network-wide scanning** patterns; vulnerable to local DoS against the host itself; can consume significant CPU processing its own data volume; and its console traffic travels **in-band**, sharing fate with the very network it's trying to protect.

### Application-Based IDS
Typically deployed on web servers, watching **user interaction** at the application layer, and — like host-based IDS — works fine against encrypted traffic.

**Disadvantages:** runs at user privilege level, making it inherently less secure than something running with elevated/kernel access.

children.title: IDS Analysis Methods — Signature vs. Anomaly Detection
children.label: IDS Analysis Methods
children.summary: Signature-based detection is precise but blind to novel attacks; anomaly detection can catch the unknown but needs a reliable definition of "normal" and tolerates more false alarms.
children.core_idea:
### Misuse (Signature-Based) Detection
Matches observed traffic against known attack signatures — often **state-based**, since many attacks unfold across multiple packets rather than a single one.

**Advantages:** few false alarms with well-written signatures; signatures can be made very tool-specific (e.g. matching the exact packet shape of a particular Nmap scan mode); easiest approach to manage day-to-day.

**Disadvantages:** only catches **known** attack patterns; every signature is a balancing act between missing real attacks (too narrow) and generating noise (too broad).

### Anomaly Detection
Builds a profile of normal use and alerts on deviation from that baseline.

| Method | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Threshold detection** | Counters on specific events (files accessed, login attempts) — e.g. is this volume of pings actually a port scan? |
| **Statistical profiles** | Formal models of what "normal" traffic/behavior looks like |
| **Rule-based models** | Explicit rules defining acceptable behavior |

**Advantages:** can catch genuinely **unknown/novel** attacks; useful as a feeder that flags candidates for a misuse-detection system to then classify.

**Disadvantages:** higher false-alarm rate than signature matching; the fundamental **training problem** — establishing a trustworthy baseline of "normal" is itself hard, especially in an environment that's already partially compromised when the baseline is built.

### IDS vs. IPS
| | IDS | IPS |
|---|---|---|
| Watches traffic for attack patterns | ✓ | ✓ |
| **Blocks** traffic based on rules | ✗ | ✓ |

### Accuracy Trade-offs
- **False positives** — flagging something that isn't actually an attack
- **False negatives** — missing a real attack entirely
- Tuning one down almost always pushes the other up; this balance is the central operational challenge of running any detection system, and large resulting log volumes are themselves hard to manage

### Before Deploying Any IDS
1. Run a **vulnerability analysis** and clean up existing issues first — an IDS deployed onto an already-compromised baseline just monitors a broken system
2. **Identify critical resources** that most need coverage
3. **Plan protections** for those specific resources rather than trying to cover everything uniformly from day one

### Snort (Open-Source NIDS)
Rule structure: **Rule Header + Rule Options**. Header actions include `Alert`, `Pass`, `Log`, `Activate`, `Dynamic`, plus protocol and port matching.

children.title: Honeypots, HoneyNets & Padded Cells
children.label: Honeypots, HoneyNets & Padded
children.summary: A honeypot is a single decoy system; a HoneyNet emulates an entire network; a padded cell redirects a detected attacker into an isolated environment mid-attack.
children.core_idea:
| Concept | Description |
|---|---|
| **Honeypot** | A single system deliberately made to look worth breaking into, with varying levels of interaction/data collection |
| **HoneyNet** | The same concept scaled up — an entire **emulated network** rather than one host |
| **Padded Cell** | Works alongside a live IDS — once an attack is detected, the attacker's traffic is transparently switched into a protected, isolated environment instead of being cut off outright |

### Advantages
Diverts an attacker away from real production systems, buys defenders time to respond, enables detailed monitoring/logging of attacker tools and techniques, and is particularly useful for surfacing **insider threats** that wouldn't trigger perimeter-focused controls.

### Disadvantages
Possible **legal exposure** (entrapment concerns depending on jurisdiction and how the honeypot is presented), uncertain general effectiveness against a sophisticated adversary who fingerprints honeypots, the risk of provoking a more aggressive response once an attacker realizes they've been deceived, and real complexity to build and maintain convincingly.

children.title: Snort — Signature-Based IDS Rules
children.label: Snort
children.summary: Snort matches packet payload and headers against rule syntax — fast and precise for known attacks, blind to anything novel.
children.core_idea:
### Rule Format
```
action protocol src_ip src_port -> dst_ip dst_port (options)
```
- **action** — `alert`, `pass`, `log`, `activate`, `dynamic`
- **options** — `content` (payload match), `sid` (rule ID), `rev` (revision number), among many others

### Practical Notes
- Fast to evaluate and highly precise against **known** attack patterns, by nature blind to genuinely novel behavior
- Tune detection thresholds carefully — overly broad content matches generate excessive noise, defeating the purpose of a "few false alarm" signature-based approach

children.title: Sigma — Portable Detection Rules
children.label: Sigma
children.summary: Sigma's YAML format converts to Splunk, Elastic, and Sentinel queries, letting detection logic be shared across SIEM platforms instead of rewritten per tool.
children.core_idea:
Write detection logic once in Sigma's generic YAML format, then convert it to the query syntax of whichever SIEM you actually run (Splunk SPL, Elastic KQL/EQL, Microsoft Sentinel, etc.) — avoids maintaining parallel, drifting rule sets across platforms.

- Map each rule to its corresponding **MITRE ATT&CK** technique tags for coverage tracking
- Version rules with an explicit `status` field (experimental/test/stable) so detection maturity is visible at a glance
- Test every rule against representative log samples before promoting it to production — a rule that's never fired against real data is an unverified assumption, not a working detection

children.title: SIEM — Correlation Use Cases
children.label: SIEM
children.summary: SIEM value comes from correlating events across sources — a single failed login is noise, but failed-then-success-from-a-new-geo is a signal.
children.core_idea:
### High-Value Correlation Patterns
- **Auth failures followed by success from a new geography** — suggests a successful brute-force or credential-stuffing attempt rather than a legitimate user simply mistyping a password
- **Impossible travel** — logins from geographically distant locations within a timeframe no real user could physically travel
- **Privilege escalation sequences** — a chain of individually-unremarkable actions that together indicate an account gaining access it shouldn't have

### Operational Practices
- **Normalize all timestamps to UTC** before correlation — timezone mismatches between log sources are a common source of both false negatives and false alibi-breaking errors (see the digital forensics domain's Autopsy case study for a concrete example of this exact failure mode)
- **Define use cases before ingesting data**, not after — undirected log collection without a correlation goal in mind produces volume without insight
- **Measure MTTD/MTTR** (Mean Time to Detect / Mean Time to Respond) per rule to know which detections are actually earning their operational cost

### Authentication-Specific Indicators Worth Correlating
A breached authentication system can go entirely undetected without dedicated monitoring — detection completes the defense loop that prevention alone cannot close:
- Impossible travel (login from two distant locations in a short window)
- Abnormal Kerberos Ticket Granting Service (TGS) request patterns
- Excessive or unusual MFA prompts (a signal of MFA-fatigue attacks)
- Ticket lifetime anomalies — tickets used well outside their expected validity window

children.title: Incident Response Lifecycle (NIST)
children.label: Incident Response Lifecycle

children.title: Core Security Vocabulary — Vulnerability, Threat, Attack, Risk
children.label: Core Security Vocabulary
children.summary: A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is potential harm; an attack is a threat carried out — precise vocabulary that underlies every policy and risk discussion.
children.core_idea:
### Definitions
- **Vulnerability** — a weakness that, if exploited, compromises one of the CIA properties:
  - Corrupted → loss of **integrity** (the asset no longer does its intended function correctly)
  - Leaky → loss of **confidentiality** (information is disclosed to unauthorized parties)
  - Unavailable/very slow → loss of **availability** (legitimate users can't access the asset)
- **Threat** — the *potential* for a security harm to an asset; not yet realized
- **Attack** — a threat that has been **carried out**, leading to an actual violation of security policy
  - **Passive attack** — attempts to learn or make use of information from a system without affecting its state (e.g. eavesdropping)
  - **Active attack** — attempts to alter system state or resources (e.g. modifying data, denial of service)
- **Security Policy** — the set of rules and regulations specifying how an organization protects its assets; vulnerabilities, threats, and attacks are all defined relative to violating this policy

### Why This Matters
Precise terminology avoids conflating "we have a vulnerability" (a weakness exists) with "we're under attack" (someone is actively exploiting it) — risk communication and incident response both depend on keeping these distinct.

children.title: AAA Model — Authentication, Authorization, Auditing
children.label: AAA Model
children.summary: Access control has three pillars: verifying identity (authentication), granting permission (authorization), and independently reviewing what happened (auditing).
children.core_idea:
### What Is Access Control?
The "gatekeeper" side of a system — everything that governs what a given identity is allowed to do.

### The Three A's
- **Authentication** — verifying that presented credentials are valid ("are you who you claim to be?")
- **Authorization** — granting a validated entity permission to access a specific resource ("are you allowed to do this?")
- **Audit** — independent review of system records to test whether controls are working, ensure compliance, and detect breaches after the fact

### Subjects & Objects
- **Subject** — the entity requesting access; further classified as **owner**, **group**, or **world** (the classic Unix permission model)
- **Object** — the resource being protected, to which access is being controlled

Authentication and authorization are enforced *in the moment*; auditing is what lets you catch failures of the first two after the fact — all three are necessary for a complete access-control story.

children.title: Information Assurance — The Four Pillars
children.label: Information Assurance
children.summary: | Pillar | Goal | |---|---| | **Confidentiality** | Information is accessible only to authorized parties | | **Integrity** | Information is accurate and has not been altered without authorization | | **Availability** |…
children.core_idea:
| Pillar | Goal |
|---|---|
| **Confidentiality** | Information is accessible only to authorized parties |
| **Integrity** | Information is accurate and has not been altered without authorization |
| **Availability** | Systems and data are accessible to legitimate users when needed |
| **Policy / Privacy** | Governs how data is handled and who is permitted to access it |

### Networking Realities That Undermine These Pillars
- A vulnerability in a single **application** can take just that app offline; a vulnerability in the **OS** can take down the entire host — the blast radius scales with the layer compromised
- **Addressing is a weak point** — every device needs a MAC address for its local segment, and IP addresses provide global uniqueness at the network layer, but **neither is verified**. An attacker can spoof any source address they choose, which undermines any control that trusts an address as a proxy for identity
- **TCP** is connection-oriented and reliable; **UDP** is connectionless and faster but gives no delivery guarantee — the choice between them is itself a security-relevant design decision (UDP-based protocols are easier to spoof and amplify)
- **Port numbers** identify which application on a host should receive traffic (80 = HTTP, 443 = HTTPS, etc.)

### Devices, By Trust Model
- **Hub** — broadcasts every packet to all connected devices; every machine on the segment can see all traffic (bad for confidentiality)
- **Switch** — forwards frames only to the intended destination
- **Router** — connects networks, forwarding based on destination IP and routing-table metrics; routers only need to know what their immediate neighbors can reach, not the full topology of the internet

children.title: Password Attack Patterns & Mitigations
children.label: Password Attack Patterns &
children.summary: Different password attack patterns call for different defenses — account lockouts stop credential stuffing, but can themselves become a denial-of-service vector.
children.core_idea:
| Attack Pattern | Description | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| **Popular Password Attack** | Try a small set of very common passwords against many accounts | Block/rate-limit computers making many rapid login attempts |
| **Password Guessing Against a Single User** | Focused brute-force / dictionary attack on one account | User training in password selection; enforce complexity/length |
| **Computer Hijacking** | Attacker gains control of an already-authenticated session | Auto-logout on inactivity |
| **Exploiting User Mistakes** | Social engineering, phishing (LFA-style credential harvesting) | User awareness training |

### Account Lockout Trade-off
Locking an account after N failed attempts stops brute-forcing, but it also hands an attacker a cheap **denial-of-service** lever — deliberately triggering lockouts on legitimate users' accounts. Modern practice favors **rate-limiting and exponential backoff** or **CAPTCHA challenges** over hard lockouts, and phishing-resistant MFA over relying on password strength alone.

children.title: Honeypots
children.label: Honeypots
children.summary: A honeypot is a deliberately vulnerable system with fake data, designed to attract attackers, waste their time, and generate high-confidence alerts.
children.core_idea:
### What Is a Honeypot?
A system left **intentionally vulnerable** — default settings, missing patches, known misconfigurations — with fake data planted on it to make it resemble a plausible, valuable target for an attacker.

### Why They Work
- No legitimate user has any reason to touch a honeypot, so **any interaction with it is a strong signal of malicious activity** — a very low false-positive detection source compared to production-network alerts
- They can absorb attacker time and effort that would otherwise be spent probing real assets
- Observed attacker behavior against a honeypot (tools, techniques, timing) feeds threat intelligence without risking real data

### Caveats
- A honeypot only helps if attackers actually find and engage with it — poorly placed or obviously fake honeypots provide no value
- Sophisticated attackers may fingerprint and avoid known honeypot signatures

children.title: Threat Actor Sophistication & Organization
children.label: Threat Actor Sophistication &
children.summary: Attackers range from script kiddies using off-the-shelf tools to state-sponsored APTs that patiently target specific high-value organizations.
children.core_idea:
### Levels of Expertise
| Level | Description |
|---|---|
| **Script Kiddie** | Minimal technical skill, uses existing off-the-shelf tools — comprises the largest share of attackers and is the easiest category to defend against |
| **Amateur** | Some real skill, often opportunistic rather than targeted |
| **Professional / APT** | Skilled, well-resourced, and targeted — see below |

### Organizational Structure
Individual actor → cause-based group → loose collective (e.g. hacktivist groups) → organized criminal enterprise (run like a business) → state-based actor, which itself splits into **state-supported**, **state-sponsored**, and **state-run** operations depending on how directly the government controls it.

### Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)
- Selects specific, high-value targets and waits patiently for an opening — a misconfiguration, a missed patch — rather than opportunistically scanning broadly
- Also targets **employees directly** via phishing: credential theft, drive-by malware downloads, malicious attachments
- **Typical APT targets:** critical infrastructure (water, power, transport), financial institutions, and organizations holding valuable IP (agriculture, manufacturing, advanced technology)

### Why Adversaries Prefer Cyber Operations
Compared to physical operations, cyber attacks offer: **reach** (remote, global targeting), **anonymity** (harder to trace, lower legal/physical risk), **cost efficiency** (major disruption for a fraction of the resources), **speed** (exploit before a patch lands), **scalability** (same tooling scales from one victim to an entire nation), and easy **reconnaissance** (scanning, OSINT on employees, data discovery) — combined with modern infrastructure's deep and growing digital dependence.

children.title: Attack Surface — Physical, Network & Third-Party Access Vectors
children.label: Attack Surface
children.summary: Attack surface spans physical access to devices, network-based access, and third-party/insider paths — each split further into deliberate vs. accidental exposure.
children.core_idea:
| Access Type | Mode | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical** | At rest | Accessing a stored device or file directly |
| **Physical** | In motion | Lost laptops, improperly discarded storage media |
| **3rd-Party Physical** | Deliberate | A malicious insider with legitimate physical access |
| **3rd-Party Physical** | Accidental | An untrained insider mishandling sensitive data |
| **Network** | Active | Direct break-in or exploitation |
| **Network** | Passive | Traffic sniffing / eavesdropping |
| **Network** | Social | Using network-based deception to get a third party to expose data themselves |

This framing is useful for threat modeling: for any asset, walk each row and ask whether that specific access mode is realistically open to an attacker, rather than treating "attack surface" as a single undifferentiated blob.

children.title: Why Authentication Really Fails
children.label: Why Authentication Really Fails
children.summary: Authentication almost never fails because the cryptography broke — it fails at the structural boundaries between trust assumptions and human behavior.
children.core_idea:
- **Authentication fails structurally, not cryptographically** — the math behind modern authentication schemes rarely breaks; what breaks are the trust assumptions surrounding it and the humans operating within it
- Most real-world compromises exploit the **boundaries between failure categories** — e.g. a technically sound cryptographic scheme undermined by a social-engineered help-desk reset, or a correct protocol running on top of an over-trusted network identity
- Compromising authentication is rarely the end goal itself — it's the enabler for **lateral movement** and establishing **persistence** inside a target environment
- Resilience requires **layered controls plus active detection** — no single authentication control is sufficient on its own; assume any one layer can fail and design for that
- Given how much downstream access depends on it, **authentication should be treated as a strategic target** in its own right when designing defenses, not as a checkbox

children.title: Buffer Overflow — Stack Layout
children.label: Buffer Overflow
children.summary: Overflowing a stack buffer can overwrite the saved return address — the classic path to arbitrary code execution before modern mitigations.
children.core_idea:
### Stack Layout (typical, growing downward)
```
[ buffer ] → [ saved EBP/RBP ] → [ saved return address ]
```
Writing past the end of `buffer` overwrites adjacent stack data — eventually reaching the saved return address, which lets an attacker redirect execution once the function returns.

### Modern Mitigations
- **ASLR** (Address Space Layout Randomization) — randomizes memory layout so an attacker can't reliably predict addresses
- **Stack canaries** — a known value placed before the return address; checked before returning, and if it's been clobbered by an overflow, execution is aborted
- **NX/DEP** (No-eXecute / Data Execution Prevention) — marks the stack non-executable, so injected shellcode can't simply run from the overflowed buffer

### Bypass Techniques
- **ROP (Return-Oriented Programming)** — chain existing executable code fragments instead of injecting new code, defeating NX
- **Info leaks** — separately leak a memory address to defeat ASLR, then combine with a controlled overwrite

children.title: ROP — Return-Oriented Programming
children.label: ROP
children.summary: Chaining existing code gadgets ending in `ret` lets an attacker execute arbitrary logic (like a syscall) even when NX blocks injected shellcode.
children.core_idea:
### Core Idea
Since NX/DEP prevents executing injected shellcode directly on the stack, ROP instead reuses tiny fragments of **already-executable** code ("gadgets") already present in the binary or its linked libraries — each gadget ends in a `ret` instruction, which pops the next gadget's address off the stack and jumps to it, chaining arbitrary sequences of operations.

### Typical Workflow
1. Find usable gadgets in the target binary and its loaded libraries
2. Chain them to set up arguments and call a useful function — commonly `mprotect` (to re-mark a memory region executable) or `execve` (to spawn a shell)
3. Point the corrupted return address at the start of the chain

### Defenses
- **CET (Control-flow Enforcement Technology)** — hardware-assisted shadow stack and indirect-branch tracking
- **Shadow stack** — a separate, protected copy of return addresses that can't be corrupted by a normal buffer overflow
- **High-entropy ASLR** — makes gadget addresses harder to locate reliably

children.title: Spectre & Meltdown — CPU Side Channels
children.label: Spectre & Meltdown
children.summary: Speculative execution can leak data across isolation boundaries via cache-timing side channels; mitigations trade performance for safety.
children.core_idea:
### The Core Issue
Modern CPUs speculatively execute instructions ahead of confirming they're actually needed, for performance. If a speculative path touches secret data before being rolled back, traces of that access can leak through **cache timing** — even though the speculative result itself is architecturally discarded.

### Meltdown
Lets an unprivileged user process **read kernel memory** by exploiting out-of-order execution that briefly accesses privileged memory before the permission check completes.

### Spectre
Tricks a *victim* process into speculatively executing code that accesses secret data conditioned on attacker-influenced branch prediction, then infers the secret via a cache-timing side channel — harder to fully patch since it exploits legitimate speculative execution rather than a specific implementation bug.

### Mitigations
- **KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation)** — separates kernel and user page tables to close the Meltdown-style read path
- **Retpoline** — a compiler technique that replaces indirect branches with a construct that resists speculative misprediction
- Microcode/OS patches for specific variants, generally at a measurable **performance cost**
- Strong isolation between mutually-untrusting workloads (e.g. separate physical hosts for sensitive multi-tenant VMs) reduces exposure where patch-level mitigation isn't enough

children.title: OSINT — Passive Reconnaissance Toolkit
children.label: OSINT
children.summary: Passive recon builds a target profile using only publicly available information — no packets sent to the target itself.
children.core_idea:
### Why Passive First
Passive reconnaissance never touches the target directly, so it can't be detected or logged by them — always the starting point before any active scanning.

### Techniques
- **Company website analysis** — staff bios, org charts, and technology mentions often leak useful details (employee names for username guessing, vendor names, internal jargon). Public-facing sites built on common CMSs (WordPress, Drupal) reveal a known attack surface just from the platform choice
- **WHOIS** — registrant, admin/technical contacts, registrar, and netrange for a domain
- **DNS enumeration** — subdomain discovery via certificate transparency logs (`crt.sh`), passive DNS aggregators (`dnsdumpster`), and tools like `viewdns.info`
- **Document metadata** — PDFs/Office docs often embed author names, software versions, and internal usernames in metadata, harvestable in bulk with tools like `exiftool` or `FOCA`
- **Social media & professional networks** — job postings reveal internal tech stacks; employee profiles reveal org structure and potential social-engineering targets
- **Search engine dorking and Shodan** (below) — indexed content and internet-wide banner scanning without ever probing the target's infrastructure yourself

### From Passive to Active
Once a profile is built, active techniques (port scanning, service enumeration — see the Nmap reference below) fill in the technical detail that passive sources can't provide, at the cost of leaving a trace on the target's side.

children.title: Nmap — Scanning Techniques Reference
children.label: Nmap
children.summary: Nmap's scan types trade off speed, stealth, and accuracy differently — SYN scans are fast and quiet, connect scans are reliable but noisier, and NSE scripts extend it into vulnerability scanning.
children.core_idea:
### Targets
```
nmap 1.2.3.4              # single IP
nmap 1.2.3.4/24            # CIDR range
nmap 1.2.3.4-8              # IP range
```
Without an explicit port range, Nmap scans the **1000 most common ports** by default.

### Host Discovery
- Default discovery mixes ICMP echo, TCP SYN to port 443, TCP ACK to port 80, and ICMP timestamp requests to determine if a host is up before scanning it
- **`-Pn`** — skip host discovery entirely and assume the target is up; use this when ICMP is blocked but services still respond normally

### Scan Types
| Flag | Name | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `-sT` | TCP Connect | Completes the full 3-way handshake — reliable, but appears as a full connection in target logs; doesn't require root |
| `-sS` | SYN ("stealth") | Sends SYN, waits for SYN-ACK, then sends RST instead of completing the handshake — faster and historically less likely to be logged as a full connection. **Requires root** for raw socket access |
| `-sF` | FIN Scan | Sends a lone FIN packet; relies on RFC-compliant systems responding differently to closed vs. open ports |
| `-sX` | XMAS Scan | Sets FIN, PSH, and URG flags together ("lit up like a Christmas tree") |
| `-sN` | Null Scan | No flags set at all |
| `-sP` / `-sn` | Ping Scan | Host discovery only, no port scan |
| `-sU` | UDP Scan | Slower and less reliable than TCP scanning — no handshake to confirm state |
| `-sA` | ACK Scan | Used to map firewall rule sets (distinguishes filtered vs. unfiltered) rather than open/closed |

**Reading port states:** Open → SYN/ACK response. Closed → RST response. Filtered → no response or ICMP unreachable (a firewall is likely dropping the probe silently). Unfiltered → response received but state indeterminate (common with ACK scans).

### Service & OS Detection
- **`-sV`** — probes open ports for banners to determine service/version
- **`-O`** — fingerprints the TCP/IP stack behavior to guess the target OS
- **`-A`** — aggressive mode: bundles OS detection, version detection, script scanning, and traceroute together
- **`-v`** — increase verbosity

### NSE (Nmap Scripting Engine)
Scripts live in `/usr/share/nmap/scripts` and run with `--script <name>`. Common categories: firewall-bypass techniques, FTP/DNS enumeration scripts, brute-force testing modules, and vulnerability-detection scripts — extending Nmap well beyond simple port scanning into lightweight vulnerability assessment.

### Output Formats
| Flag | Format |
|---|---|
| `-oN` | Normal text output |
| `-oX` | XML |
| `-oG` | Grepable (legacy, largely unused now) |
| `-oS` | "Script kiddie" novelty format |

commands.explain: Stealth SYN scan with service/version detection, OS fingerprinting, and default scripts.
Skip host discovery and scan all 65535 ports — useful when ICMP is filtered.
Run NSE's vulnerability-detection script category against a target.

children.title: Shodan — Internet Asset Discovery
children.label: Shodan
children.summary: Shodan indexes banners and service metadata across the internet — useful for finding exposed ICS, RDP, and default-credential interfaces without touching the target directly.
children.core_idea:
Shodan continuously scans the internet and indexes what it finds — banners, service metadata, and (for many devices) default configuration fingerprints — letting you search that index rather than scanning yourself.

- Query by organization, product name, or known vulnerability tag
- Pair any Shodan-driven investigation with clear **legal scope** — you're searching a third party's index, but acting on what you find against a system you don't control still carries the same legal exposure as scanning it directly
- Complements active `nmap` scanning nicely: use Shodan to find exposed assets first, then run targeted active scans only against in-scope CIDR ranges

children.title: Google Dorking — Search Operator OSINT
children.label: Google Dorking
children.summary: Advanced search operators like site:, filetype:, and inurl: surface indexed files, login pages, and error messages that reveal information about a target.
children.core_idea:
| Operator | Finds |
|---|---|
| `site:target.com` | Restrict results to a specific domain |
| `filetype:pdf` | Restrict to a file type — combine with `site:` to find exposed documents |
| `inurl:admin login` | Pages with specific terms in the URL — useful for locating admin panels |

**Example:** `site:target.com filetype:pdf` surfaces every indexed PDF on a domain — often internal reports or presentations never meant to be public.

A target's own `robots.txt` and cached pages are also worth checking directly — `robots.txt` sometimes lists paths the site owner explicitly wanted hidden from crawlers (which paradoxically flags them as interesting), and Google's cache can reveal content that's since been removed from the live site.

children.title: Malware Taxonomy — Viruses, Worms, Trojans & Ransomware
children.label: Malware Taxonomy
children.summary: Malware is classified by how it spreads: viruses need a host program, worms self-replicate independently, and Trojans/ransomware rely on deception rather than replication.
children.core_idea:
### Classification by Replication Mechanism
| Type | Needs a Host Program? | Self-Replicates? |
|---|---|---|
| **Virus** | Yes — attaches to and requires a host program to spread | Yes, but only via the host |
| **Worm** | No — independent, self-contained | Yes, spreads autonomously across a network |
| **Trojan** | No | No — relies on tricking a user into running it |
| **Bot** | No | Often yes, as part of a coordinated botnet |

### Countermeasures Against Self-Replicating Malware
- **Antivirus software** — signature and heuristic-based detection
- **Network segmentation** — limits how far a worm can spread once inside
- **Consumer/system hardening** — patching known propagation vectors before a worm can exploit them

### Ransomware Delivery Note
Ransomware that bypasses network-based mitigations typically does so by first landing on a **trusted, already-compromised host inside the business network** — once inside the trust boundary, network-perimeter controls that only inspect north-south (in/out) traffic have far less visibility into what that host does next.

children.title: CherryBlos — Mobile Banking Trojan Case Study
children.label: CherryBlos
children.summary: CherryBlos combined OCR-based credential theft (scanning photo galleries for crypto seed phrases) with Accessibility Service abuse to overlay fake screens on real banking apps.
children.core_idea:
### Background
Discovered by Trend Micro in mid-2023 (MITRE ATT&CK Software ID: **S1225**). A multi-stage Android malware family with an unusually creative theft mechanism.

### Objective
Direct financial theft, specifically targeting **cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases** rather than conventional data like emails or documents.

### OCR-Based Theft
CherryBlos used **Optical Character Recognition** to scan a victim's photo gallery for screenshots containing crypto wallet seed phrases. Despite repeated platform warnings against it, users commonly screenshot their recovery phrases during wallet setup — CherryBlos automated the search for these "digital master keys" across the entire gallery.

### Accessibility Service Abuse
The malware social-engineered victims into enabling Android's **Accessibility Services** (designed for users with disabilities), then abused those elevated permissions to auto-approve further permission requests and to **overlay fake login screens on top of real banking apps**, harvesting credentials as the victim typed them into what looked like the genuine app.

### Takeaway
A useful case study in how legitimate accessibility/OS features become high-value abuse targets once granted — and why "screenshot your recovery phrase" is specifically the kind of user habit malware authors design around.

children.title: Cyber-Enabled Adversary Goals — Money, Data, Disruption, Influence
children.label: Cyber
children.summary: Adversary goals cluster into five categories — money, data, disruption, influence, and public trust — and are frequently pursued together.
children.core_idea:
| Goal | Mechanisms |
|---|---|
| **Money** | Direct theft (account takeover, redirecting funds, purchase fraud), ransomware, extortion |
| **Data** | PII, medical records, IP, and operational/infrastructure plans — targeted for disclosure, reuse (identity theft, account access), or as a stepping stone toward a larger attack; can also be held hostage |
| **Disruption** | Physical services (power, water, traffic, gas, building controls, medical devices) or IT services (911 systems, government services, communications) — used either as ransom leverage or as the end goal itself (terror/chaos) |
| **Influence** | Personal (swatting, fake kidnapping claims, direct threats — usually paired with a money demand) or public (aimed purely at fear/chaos, not necessarily financial gain) |
| **Public Trust** | Eroding confidence in governments, elected officials, public services, elections, or corporate brands |

These goals are rarely pursued in isolation — a ransomware attack, for example, simultaneously chases **money** (extortion) and **disruption** (as the leverage that makes the extortion work).

children.title: Real-World Cyber-Physical Attack Case Studies
children.label: Real
children.summary: From Stuxnet to the Colonial Pipeline, these incidents show attackers moving from data theft into physical-world consequences.
children.core_idea:
| Incident | What Happened |
|---|---|
| **Target (2013)** | Attackers gained credentials via a compromised HVAC contractor, installed memory-scraping malware on POS terminals, and stole millions of credit card numbers |
| **Sony Pictures (2014)** | Believed to be an APT; entry point unclear. One of the first attacks to cause widespread destruction of computing resources, combining data theft with operational disruption |
| **Turkish Pipeline (2008)** | One of the earliest known cyber-physical attacks — gained access via internet-connected cameras, altered pipeline pressure settings, and disabled monitoring |
| **Iranian Centrifuges — Stuxnet** | Malware manipulated centrifuge sensor data to cause physical damage while reporting normal readings to operators — exploited process-level vulnerabilities, not just IT ones |
| **Ukraine Power Grid** | Russian-attributed attack causing widespread power outages |
| **Colonial Pipeline (2021)** | Ransomware disrupted business IT systems severely enough to halt fuel distribution across the U.S. East Coast, despite the ransomware itself not touching OT/pipeline control systems directly |
| **Florida Water Treatment Plant (2021)** | Attacker gained remote access and attempted to raise sodium hydroxide (lye) to dangerous concentrations |
| **2016 DNC Email Leak** | Spear phishing led to leaked emails that influenced public opinion during a presidential election — an influence-goal attack, not a financial one |
| **2020 Twitter Bitcoin Scam** | Insiders were social-engineered into granting access to high-profile verified accounts, used to run a cryptocurrency scam at scale |

**Pattern:** the highest-consequence incidents (Stuxnet, Florida, Ukraine, Colonial Pipeline) all involve crossing from the IT domain into physical/OT consequences — the common thread worth remembering when scoping "worst case" for critical infrastructure.

children.title: Browser Lock / Tech Support Scams
children.label: Browser Lock / Tech
children.summary: A malicious page traps the browser with a loud fake infection warning and a support number, pressuring victims into paying for fictitious remediation.
children.core_idea:
### How It Works
1. **Trigger** — victim visits a compromised or intentionally malicious website
2. **Scare tactic** — a pop-up (often with an alarming auto-playing voice) claims the computer is infected with a virus or ransomware
3. **Lockdown effect** — the browser becomes unresponsive, or the pop-up reappears in a loop, creating the illusion the machine is genuinely locked
4. **Urgency & payment** — the message pushes the victim to call a "tech support" number immediately, where they're pressured into paying for fake remediation (or granting remote access that enables real compromise)

### Why It Works
Combines urgency, authority framing (fake Microsoft/Apple branding), and a plausible-sounding threat to override a typical user's usual caution — the browser lock itself is just a UI trick (a JavaScript loop or fullscreen overlay), not an actual infection, but victims rarely realize that in the moment.

### Mitigation
- User education: a real OS/AV infection alert never asks you to call a phone number
- Force-close via task manager rather than interacting with the page at all
- Keep browsers patched — some variants pair the social-engineering lock with an actual exploit attempt

children.title: Business Email Compromise (BEC) — Mechanics & Defense
children.label: Business Email Compromise
children.summary: BEC and its individual-targeting counterpart EAC consistently rank among the costliest cybercrime categories, working by inserting into or fabricating a trusted relationship.
children.core_idea:
### Scale of the Problem
Social engineering is estimated to be behind **over 60% of data loss incidents**. **BEC** targets businesses specifically; **EAC (Email Account Compromise)** uses the same methods against individuals — BEC/EAC together are consistently among the costliest cybercrime categories reported (IC3 Annual Report).

### Entry Point 1 — Inserting Into an Existing Relationship
- **Compromising a valid account** via password guessing, a phishing email (often just the first step toward a bigger objective), or malware planted via drive-by download or direct credential theft
- Once inside, the attacker still needs to **groom** the victim/counterparty before making the actual ask — jumping straight to a fraudulent request from a "legitimate" account raises suspicion
- **Video calls** are an emerging vector — the attacker joins a meeting impersonating a known participant, lending real-time credibility a text-only phish can't match

### Entry Point 2 — Fabricating a New Relationship
- A fake email address (one-off financial ask, or an ongoing impersonation of a bank/partner company, often paired with interactive "grooming" conversation)
- A phone call using spoofed caller ID for interactive social engineering
- A text message, often aimed at credential theft
- A video call, again pretending to be a company representative

### Mitigation Layers
- **Technology** — email/malware scanners, DMARC/SPF/DKIM enforcement, tagging external senders
- **User education** — never underestimate an attacker's ability to fool a trained user; awareness has to be continuous, not a once-a-year training
- **Process** — secure, verified-out-of-band procedures for any money transfer or sensitive request, so no single email (however convincing) can authorize a transaction alone

### Three-Level Training Plan
Technology slows attacks but the workforce is the real control surface:
1. **Cybersecurity literacy** — baseline cyber hygiene for everyone
2. **Hands-on technical training** — role-specific, practical skills
3. **Cyber planning exercises** — tabletop/simulation of an actual incident response

children.title: YARA — Pattern Matching for Malware
children.label: YARA
children.summary: YARA rules match strings, hex patterns, or regex with boolean conditions, letting you scan files, memory, or traffic for malware signatures at scale.
children.core_idea:
### Rule Structure
```
rule ExampleRule {
    meta:
        author = "analyst"
        description = "..."
    strings:
        $s1 = "malicious_string"
        $hex1 = { E8 ?? ?? ?? ?? }
    condition:
        $s1 or $hex1
}
```
- **meta** — free-form metadata, not evaluated
- **strings** — text, hex byte patterns (with wildcards `??`), or regex to search for
- **condition** — boolean logic over the defined strings (`and`/`or`/counts/`all of them`)

Use the built-in **`pe` module** for structural PE-header conditions (imports, sections, entry point) instead of relying purely on byte patterns.

### Practice
Always test a new rule against a large corpus of **known-clean** files to measure its false-positive rate before deploying it in a detection pipeline.

commands.explain: Scan a file or directory against a YARA rule.
Recursively scan a directory tree.

children.title: Static vs Dynamic Malware Analysis
children.label: Static vs Dynamic Malware
children.summary: Static analysis inspects a sample without running it; dynamic analysis observes its actual behavior in an isolated sandbox — real workflows combine both.
children.core_idea:
| Approach | What It Does | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **Static** | Strings, imports, disassembly — inspected without ever executing the sample | Packers and obfuscation can hide the real logic from static tools entirely |
| **Dynamic** | Run the sample in an isolated sandbox VM, observe behavior: network IOCs, file/registry writes, API calls | Malware with anti-VM/anti-sandbox checks may detect the analysis environment and refuse to show its real behavior |

### Practical Workflow
Combine both: static analysis first for a quick triage and IOC extraction, then dynamic analysis in an isolated VM to reveal packed/obfuscated behavior — watching specifically for anti-VM checks (timing checks, hardware fingerprinting, hypervisor detection) that suggest the sample is evasive.

children.title: MITRE ATT&CK — Tactic & Technique Mapping
children.label: MITRE ATT&CK
children.summary: Mapping observed behaviors to standardized ATT&CK tactics/techniques gives detection engineering and incident reporting a common, comparable vocabulary.
children.core_idea:
### Why Map to ATT&CK
Translating raw observed behavior ("this process spawned that process and reached out to this IP") into standardized **tactic/technique IDs** makes findings comparable across incidents, tools, and organizations — instead of every report using ad hoc language for the same underlying behavior.

### Practical Uses
- Reference specific **technique IDs** inside detection rules (e.g. Sigma rules) so a rule's coverage is self-documenting
- **Detection gap analysis** — plot which techniques your current detections actually cover, and where the blind spots are
- **ATT&CK Navigator layers** — visualize coverage (or an adversary's known technique set, like CherryBlos's Software ID S1225 above) as a heatmap over the full matrix, making gaps and overlaps immediately visible
